items.prompt: What time did the call actually begin?
items.audio:
Dilnoza Karimova was sitting at her kitchen table on a rainy Tuesday morning when the phone rang. It was Mr. Henderson, the hiring manager at a small marketing agency in Leeds, calling for the first stage of the interview. He began by apologising. The call had been arranged for ten o'clock, but a client had rung him at the last minute, so he had asked his assistant to move it to ten fifteen. Dilnoza said that was no problem at all, because she had cleared her whole morning anyway.

Mr. Henderson started with the usual question about why she wanted the job. Dilnoza explained that she had spent three years as a junior copywriter in Tashkent, mostly writing product descriptions for an online shop, and that she now wanted to move into campaign planning. She added that she had not applied to a big corporation on purpose, since she felt people in small teams learn faster, because everybody does a bit of everything. Mr. Henderson laughed and said that was certainly true in his agency, where there were only fourteen employees, although last year there had been as many as twenty before two of them left to start their own company.

Then he asked about her biggest weakness. She said she used to take on too much work because she hated saying no, but that she had recently begun keeping a weekly planner, and that it had helped far more than she expected. He seemed to like that answer and said that he himself had never managed to keep a planner for more than a fortnight.

After that came the practical questions. Dilnoza thought she had heard the salary as thirteen thousand pounds, but Mr. Henderson repeated it slowly. The starting salary was thirty one thousand pounds a year, rising to thirty four thousand after the probation period of six months. Working hours were nine to five, with one day a week at home, although the agency expected everyone in the office on Thursdays for the team lunch. He also mentioned that parking was not free, so most people came by train.

Near the end, Dilnoza asked whether the post involved much travel. Mr. Henderson said it did not, apart from the occasional visit to a printing company in Manchester, perhaps four times a year. She had been worried about that because she did not have a driving licence yet, but he told her that the company would pay for train tickets, so it would not be a problem at all.

Finally he said that the second round would be a face to face meeting with the director, Mrs. Okafor, and a short writing test. It was going to be on Monday of the following week, at two o'clock. Actually, he corrected himself, his diary said half past two, because the director had a dentist appointment earlier that day. He promised to send an email confirming everything by Friday afternoon. Dilnoza thanked him, put the phone down, and decided to celebrate with a very large cup of tea.

items.prompt: What did the researchers expect to find at first?
items.answer: That remote workers would be lazy
items.audio:
Good morning, and welcome to the programme. Today Doctor Farida Rahimova, who studies workplace habits at a university in Samarkand, talks about remote work, a subject she says people discuss with far more heat than evidence. She begins by saying that when her team started the research four years ago, they expected to find that staying at home made people lazy. In fact the opposite turned out to be true. In a survey of two thousand five hundred employees, about sixty percent said they worked longer hours at home than in the office. Actually, she corrects herself, the figure was sixty six percent, and she regrets that a newspaper once printed the lower number.

The long hours, she explains, are not entirely good news. Without a commute, many people simply start earlier and finish later, and the boundary between work and private life disappears. One participant, a software tester called Bakhtiyor, told her that he answered messages at eleven at night because his laptop was sitting next to his bed. His family eventually persuaded him to keep it in the hall.

Doctor Rahimova then turns to the benefits. Most people saved around an hour and a half every day by not travelling, and about a third used part of that time to exercise. She is quick to add that this does not mean everyone is happier. Younger employees, in particular, said they felt lonely and missed learning from colleagues by simply watching them work. Several of them admitted they had not met their managers in person for more than a year.

Her own view is that the best arrangement is neither fully remote nor fully in the office. She suggests three days at home and two in the office, with the office days chosen by the team rather than the company, so that people actually meet. She admits that she used to prefer four days at home, but changed her mind after seeing how much the youngest workers struggled.

The presenter asks whether companies save money. Doctor Rahimova says that they do, but not as much as managers hope. Smaller offices cost less to rent, yet firms often spend that money on better equipment, software and sometimes a monthly allowance for home internet. A director she interviewed said the allowance was only the equivalent of twenty dollars, but that employees valued it far more than a free lunch.

Finally she warns listeners against one common mistake. Managers tend to judge people by how quickly they reply to messages, which rewards those who are always online, not those who do the best work. She recommends judging results instead. The presenter thanks her, and promises that after the news and weather, a farmer from Bukhara will explain how he runs his business using nothing but a phone.
options: That remote workers would be lazy
That remote workers would earn more

She begins by saying that when her team started the research four years ago, they expected to find that staying at home made people lazy. In fact the opposite turned out to be true. In a survey of two thousand five hundred employees, about sixty percent said they worked longer hours at home than in the office. Actually, she corrects herself, the figure was sixty six percent, and she regrets that a newspaper once printed the lower number.

The long hours, she explains, are not entirely good news. Without a commute, many people simply start earlier and finish later, and the boundary between work and private life disappears. One participant, a software tester called Bakhtiyor, told her that he answered messages at eleven at night because his laptop was sitting next to his bed. His family eventually persuaded him to keep it in the hall.

Doctor Rahimova then turns to the benefits. Most people saved around an hour and a half every day by not travelling, and about a third used part of that time to exercise. She is quick to add that this does not mean everyone is happier. Younger employees, in particular, said they felt lonely and missed learning from colleagues by simply watching them work. Several of them admitted they had not met their managers in person for more than a year.

Her own view is that the best arrangement is neither fully remote nor fully in the office. She suggests three days at home and two in the office, with the office days chosen by the team rather than the company, so that people actually meet. She admits that she used to prefer four days at home, but changed her mind after seeing how much the youngest workers struggled.

The presenter asks whether companies save money. Doctor Rahimova says that they do, but not as much as managers hope. Smaller offices cost less to rent, yet firms often spend that money on better equipment, software and sometimes a monthly allowance for home internet. A director she interviewed said the allowance was only the equivalent of twenty dollars, but that employees valued it far more than a free lunch.

Finally she warns listeners against one common mistake. Managers tend to judge people by how quickly they reply to messages, which rewards those who are always online, not those who do the best work. She recommends judging results instead. The presenter thanks her, and promises that after the news and weather, a farmer from Bukhara will explain how he runs his business using nothing but a phone.

items.prompt: When will the company actually move?
items.audio:
Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for staying a little after lunch. I know some of you have deadlines, so I will try to be quick. I want to tell you about three changes, and I would like you to hear them from me rather than from the rumour machine in the canteen.

First, the office move. As most of you know, we were going to leave this building at the end of March. Well, that is no longer going to happen. The new premises by the river will not be ready until June, because the builders found a problem with the heating system. So we stay here for another three months, which, to be honest, I do not mind, since the parking at the new place is still undecided. When we do move, the sales and customer service teams will go on the second floor, and the warehouse office will go on the ground floor, next to the loading area. The finance department is the exception. They will remain here until the autumn, because their archive is too large to move in one go.

Second, shifts. From the first of July the early shift will begin at six thirty instead of seven, not at six, as some of you have been saying. I know that half an hour sounds small, but the trucks from the port now arrive earlier, and we cannot keep them waiting. Nobody will be forced to change. Anyone who prefers the later shift can stay on it, but the later shift will finish at half past six, not at six. There will be a small bonus, forty pounds a month, for people on the early shift. I originally wanted to make it sixty, but the budget committee said no.

Third, and this is the part that worries people, restructuring. I want to be very clear: nobody is losing their job. What will happen is that the two jobs of stock controller and order coordinator will be combined into one role called operations assistant. Those currently doing either job will be offered the new post with the same pay, and training will begin in September. Anyone who does not want it can apply for another vacancy inside the company first, before we advertise outside.

I have been working here for eleven years, and I have never seen the company in such a strong position. Last year we delivered to more than two hundred customers, compared with a hundred and eighty the year before. I am not saying that change is easy. I am saying that I would not announce it if I thought it would damage the people in this room.

Now, questions. Please raise your hand, and Priya will bring you the microphone.

items.prompt: How many employers are at the fair this year?
items.audio:
Good morning, everybody, and welcome to the annual spring job fair. My name is Gulnora Tashpulatova, and I run the careers office here. Before I let you loose on the stalls, I would like to say a few words, and I promise they will be shorter than the queue outside.

First, some practical information. This year we have ninety employers, which is ten more than last year. The doors will stay open until five o'clock, not four, as it says on the posters. Somebody printed the wrong time, and I apologise. The registration desk is on your left as you come in, and you will need your student card, but not a printed CV, because the employers prefer to scan the code on your badge. If you do want a paper copy, the library will print it for free, though only until noon. The CV clinic was supposed to be in this hall, but it has been moved to the sports hall at the back of the building, since so many people signed up for it. Lunch is not included, I am afraid, but the cafe on the ground floor offers a discount to anyone wearing a badge.

Now, a story. When I graduated nine years ago, I applied for thirty jobs. I got thirteen replies, and only four of them were invitations to an interview. Not one led to an offer. I was convinced something was wrong with me. It took me a long time to understand that nothing was wrong with me, and that most people hear no far more often than they hear yes. So if somebody turns you down today, do not take it personally. Ask politely what you could improve, and move on to the next stall.

I also want to challenge an idea that you will hear a lot today, which is the dream job. I do not believe in it, or at least not at your age. In my experience, people who wait for the perfect position wait for a very long time. The people who do well take a reasonable job, learn quickly, and make themselves useful. My own first job was in a call centre, and I hated it, but I learned how to stay calm with angry customers, and I still use that skill every single week.

A word about the companies. You will find banks, hospitals, software firms and two airlines, but the stall I recommend you visit first is the small bakery chain in the corner. They are hiring eight people for management training, which is rare, and they told me they care more about attitude than grades.

Finally, a tip. Do not go straight to the company you like best. Start with one you are less interested in, so that you can warm up, make your mistakes there, and arrive at your favourite stall feeling confident. Now, please enjoy the day, and good luck.

items.prompt: How long has Margaret worked in the department?
items.audio:
Everyone, could I have your attention for a moment? Thank you. I promised Margaret that I would keep this short, and I promised the cake that I would keep it even shorter, so let me begin.

Margaret Whitfield joined this accounts department twenty five years ago, when we still kept most of our records in paper folders, and when the photocopier was the most dangerous machine in the building. Her first manager, a gentleman who has since retired to Cyprus, told me that she asked more questions in her first week than the rest of the team had asked in a year. He meant it as a complaint. Looking back, it was the best sign we could have had.

Many of you think Margaret is retiring today, and I have to correct that. She is not. She is leaving us for a job at a children's charity in Birmingham, where she will be the finance director. When she told me, I was sad, naturally, but also a little jealous, because the charity offered her a free lunch every Friday. She says that was not the reason she accepted. I choose not to believe her.

Let me tell you what she has done for us. She trained nearly forty people, including me. She introduced the monthly review meeting, which everyone hated at first and nobody can now live without. She found a mistake of about eighty thousand pounds in a supplier's invoice, and never once mentioned it afterwards, though anyone else would have put it on a poster. And when the system crashed during the year end, she stayed here until three in the morning, with a flask of tea and a calculator, and had the figures ready by eight. I remember that she was not angry. She simply said that computers come and go, but arithmetic is permanent.

Now for a confession. Margaret planned to leave in December, after the audit. Then the charity asked her to start earlier, so she is going at the end of this month, and her desk will be taken by Karim from the Leeds office. Karim is very capable, but he does not drink tea, which I consider a serious weakness, and he has asked whether the old calculator will go with Margaret. I told him no. Some things are not for sale.

Those of us who worked closely with her know that her best quality was not her skill with numbers. It was that she always had time for you. If you were struggling, she would shut her laptop, turn her chair around and say, tell me about it. That is rarer than any qualification.

So, please raise your cups, and, since there is no champagne, your tea. To Margaret: we will miss you, we will visit you, and we will expect a discount on the charity's next dinner. Thank you, Margaret.

items.prompt: Why did Zarina give up the idea of pharmacy?
items.answer: She saw a nurse calm a frightened boy
items.audio:
In this week's programme, the presenter, Daniel, talks to Zarina Yusupova, who has been a nurse on a children's ward for eleven years. Daniel begins by asking whether it is true that she nearly became a pharmacist. Zarina laughs and says that it is, because her mother wanted her to, and she had actually been accepted onto a pharmacy course. Then, during a summer job at a hospital reception, she watched a nurse calm a frightened boy simply by talking to him about football, and she changed her mind in a single afternoon.

Daniel asks about the hardest part of the job. Many people expect her to say the sad cases, but Zarina says the hardest thing is the tiredness. She works three night shifts a week, from eight in the evening until seven in the morning, and she says her body never fully adjusts. She has learned to sleep with thick curtains and a fan, and she never drinks coffee after midnight, although she admits that she used to drink four cups a night. Her doctor told her to stop, and for once she listened.

The presenter then raises the subject of pay. Zarina says that she does not think nurses are paid badly compared with teachers, but that the pay does not reflect the pressure. Then she corrects herself. Pay is not the main problem, she says, because what really drives people away is a shortage of staff. On her ward there should be nine nurses on a night shift, and often there are only six. When that happens, nobody has time to sit with a worried parent, and that, in her opinion, is the real loss.

Daniel wants to know about the best moments. She describes a little girl called Malika, who was in hospital for five weeks with a serious chest infection. On the day she went home, Malika gave her a drawing of a nurse with enormous shoes. Zarina keeps it in her locker, and says that on a bad night she looks at it for a minute before going back to work.

Asked what advice she would give to someone thinking of becoming a nurse, Zarina does not talk about studying at all. She says people should first spend a few weeks volunteering, because the job looks very different from the inside. Some people discover they cannot bear it, and it is better to find out early. Others, like her, discover they cannot imagine doing anything else.

Finally, Daniel asks whether she would like her own children to follow her. Zarina says that she has a son of eight, and that he currently wants to be a dinosaur. She will be happy with whatever he chooses, as long as it is not the night shift. Daniel thanks her, and the programme moves on to the weather.
options: She saw a nurse calm a frightened boy

topic: A meeting recap, A training course introduction, An HR voicemail, ...
title: Tinglash 3
intro: Har bir savol uchun 🔊 tugmasini bosib matnni tinglang (kerak bo'lsa qayta tinglang), so'ng javob bering.

items.prompt: Why did the meeting start late?
items.audio:
Hi Laura, I know you could not make the project meeting yesterday, so here is a recap, and I will try to keep it in order. The meeting started at nine thirty, half an hour late, because the projector refused to work and we ended up squeezing around Olga's laptop.

The first item was the launch date for the new mobile app. You will remember that we had agreed on the fifteenth of October. Well, that has changed. Sven, who leads the testing, said that his team had found more than sixty faults in the payment feature, and that it would be irresponsible to release the app before they are fixed. Olga was not happy, as she had promised the board the original date, but in the end she accepted that the launch will be on the fifth of November. Please note: fifth, not fifteenth, because I have already seen two people write it down wrongly.

The second item was budget. Rashid reported that we have spent about seventy percent of the money for the year, with only four months to go. That sounds alarming, but he explained that the most expensive part, the licence for the design software, has already been paid, so the monthly cost will be much lower from now on. He asked everyone to send him receipts by the end of the week, not the end of the month, which is what some of you usually do. I think he was looking at you, Laura, when he said it.

Third, staffing. We are going to hire two new developers, not three, as Olga first suggested. She argued for three, but Rashid pointed out that we do not have the desks, and honestly he was right. The interviews are going to be held in the week after the launch, so that nobody is distracted.

Now, what is expected of you. First, you are asked to write a short guide for customers explaining the new payment screen. Olga wants it by Thursday, but I have a feeling that she will accept Friday morning. Second, you should book the large meeting room for the launch party, although nobody has decided yet whether it will be a party or just cake and a speech. My own vote is for a party, but nobody asked me.

One more thing. There was a long discussion about working on Saturdays before the launch. Sven suggested it, and Olga looked interested for a moment, but several of us objected strongly. We said that we had done it twice this year and people were exhausted. In the end, nobody will be asked to work on Saturdays, although volunteers are welcome. I expect there will be none.

That is all I can remember. If you want the full notes, Hannah wrote them up, but fair warning: they are eleven pages long, and about half of it is about the projector.

The first item was the launch date for the new mobile app. You will remember that we had agreed on the fifteenth of October. Well, that has changed. Sven, who leads the testing, said that his team had found more than sixty faults in the payment feature, and that it would be irresponsible to release the app before they are fixed. Olga was not happy, as she had promised the board the original date, but in the end she accepted that the launch will be on the fifth of November. Please note: fifth, not fifteenth, because I have already seen two people write it down wrongly.

The second item was budget. Rashid reported that we have spent about seventy percent of the money for the year, with only four months to go. That sounds alarming, but he explained that the most expensive part, the licence for the design software, has already been paid, so the monthly cost will be much lower from now on. He asked everyone to send him receipts by the end of the week, not the end of the month, which is what some of you usually do. I think he was looking at you, Laura, when he said it.

Third, staffing. We are going to hire two new developers, not three, as Olga first suggested. She argued for three, but Rashid pointed out that we do not have the desks, and honestly he was right. The interviews are going to be held in the week after the launch, so that nobody is distracted.

Now, what is expected of you. First, you are asked to write a short guide for customers explaining the new payment screen. Olga wants it by Thursday, but I have a feeling that she will accept Friday morning. Second, you should book the large meeting room for the launch party, although nobody has decided yet whether it will be a party or just cake and a speech. My own vote is for a party, but nobody asked me.

One more thing. There was a long discussion about working on Saturdays before the launch. Sven suggested it, and Olga looked interested for a moment, but several of us objected strongly. We said that we had done it twice this year and people were exhausted. In the end, nobody will be asked to work on Saturdays, although volunteers are welcome. I expect there will be none.

That is all I can remember. If you want the full notes, Hannah wrote them up, but fair warning: they are eleven pages long, and about half of it is about the projector.

items.prompt: How long does the course last this year?
items.audio:
Welcome, everyone, and please do sit down wherever you like. My name is Joseph Okonkwo, and for the next four days I am going to be your trainer on this customer service course. Some of you were told it would last three days. That was true last year, but we added a fourth day, a Friday, devoted to practice with real customers, because last year's group asked for it.

Let me explain the structure. Monday, Tuesday and Thursday will take place here in room twelve, from nine until half past four. Wednesday is the exception: it is online, so you can follow it from home, but you will need a working camera. If your camera is broken, speak to Samira at reception today, because she has a few spare ones. Friday will be at the main hotel on the seafront, and please do not arrive late, because the manager there, Mrs. Lindqvist, has strong opinions about punctuality.

Now, what will we actually learn? I want to begin with something that may surprise you. This course is not mainly about smiling. Smiling is easy, and everyone can do it for an hour. What is difficult is staying helpful when a customer is rude, when you are tired, and when it is the end of a twelve hour shift. So on Tuesday we spend the entire morning on complaints. I will play recordings of real, very angry phone calls, and we will practise answering them. I should warn you that some of the language is strong, although nothing you have not heard at a football match.

On Thursday, we move to the subject people find hardest, which is saying no politely. When a guest asks for a late checkout and the room is already booked, you cannot just refuse. You offer an alternative, such as storing the luggage for free. A good no, I tell people, is a yes to something else.

There will be no exam, but there is a small assessment. You will be observed on Friday, and to receive the certificate you must attend at least three of the four days, and pass the Friday observation. I know some of you were hoping the certificate was automatic. It is not, I am afraid, but in eight years almost nobody has failed.

Practical matters: lunch is provided on Monday and Tuesday only. After that you are on your own, though there is a good sandwich shop on the corner. Phones are allowed, but please keep them silent. And if you are the sort of person who never asks questions in a group, please try, because last year the best questions came from the quietest people.

Right, let us start with a short introduction. Tell the person next to you your name, your job, and the most unreasonable request a customer has ever made to you. I will go first: a man once asked me to move the sea closer to his window.

items.prompt: Why is Helen leaving a voicemail?
items.answer: She could not reach Bobur on his mobile
items.audio:
Hello, Bobur, this is Helen Marsh from human resources at Northgate Logistics. I am leaving you this message because I have tried your mobile twice this morning and I think it must be switched off. First of all, congratulations again on accepting the offer. We are all delighted that you are joining us.

Right, let me go through what you need to know before you start. Your first day is Monday the third. I think the letter we sent says the tenth, but that was a mistake on our side, and I apologise for the confusion. Please come to the main reception on the ground floor at eight forty five, not nine, because security needs time to take your photograph for your pass. Ask for me, and if I am not there, ask for my colleague Adrian, who is much friendlier than he looks.

Now, documents. You will need to bring your passport or your national identity card, but not both, and also your bank details so that we can set up your salary. Please do not send them by email. Bring them in person, written down or on a card, and I will enter them myself. We also need a proof of address from the last three months, such as a utility bill. A mobile phone bill is not accepted, I am afraid, although a bank statement is fine. If you have a driving licence, bring it too, since you will be moving between our two warehouses, but you will not have to drive in the first week.

About the first week itself. On Monday you will have a general induction with five other new staff, and it finishes at noon. After that you will have lunch with your team leader, Gulshan, who has asked me to tell you that she is paying, so please order whatever you like, within reason. On Tuesday you start the safety training, which takes the whole day, and you will be given boots and a jacket. Please tell me your boot size, because last time somebody guessed and we ended up with a gentleman wearing shoes two sizes too small. Forty three, forty four, I need to know which. Please ring me back or send a text, and just a number is enough.

One last thing, and it is a little awkward. We said that the salary would be paid on the twenty fifth of each month. That is still true, but for your very first month the payment will be a few days later, probably on the thirtieth, because of the way our payroll works. I know that is annoying if you have bills waiting, so if it causes a problem, please tell me and we will see if we can arrange an advance.

My direct number is on the letter, but let me say it differently. Just call the main switchboard and ask for Helen in human resources. Right, I think that is everything. Looking forward to seeing you on the third. Goodbye, and have a lovely weekend.

items.prompt: How long has Leo been freelancing?
items.audio:
Welcome back to the podcast. This week Kamila, who hosts the show, is talking to Leo Marchetti, a graphic designer who left a stable office job three years ago and has been freelancing ever since. Kamila starts by asking the question everyone wants answered: was it worth it? Leo pauses, then says the honest answer is yes, but not for the reason he expected. He thought freedom would be the main benefit, whereas the real gift turned out to be learning how to value his own time.

He explains that his first year was a disaster. He accepted every project that came along, charged very little, and worked weekends. At one point he was earning less than in his old job, and he seriously thought about going back. Kamila asks what changed. Leo says it was a conversation with an older freelancer, a photographer, who told him that cheap clients are the most demanding. So he raised his prices by a third, and, to his surprise, lost only one client out of seven, and that client had been paying late anyway.

The conversation turns to money, which Kamila says is the topic freelancers fear most. Leo gives three rules. First, always ask for a deposit, usually thirty percent, before starting. Second, put everything in writing, including the number of revisions, because without a limit a client may ask for changes forever. Third, keep enough savings for three months, and he stresses that this does not mean three months of profit, it means three months of living costs. He admits that he ignored the third rule at the start, and spent one very stressful winter eating pasta.

Kamila asks about loneliness. Leo says that he feared it more than anything but that it is less of a problem than expected, as long as he leaves the flat. He rents a desk in a shared workspace twice a week, where there is a coffee machine, a bad printer and a surprisingly good chess club. He did not go to the club for a year because he thought chess was boring, and now he plays every Friday.

Then comes a more critical moment. Kamila suggests that freelancing is the future of work. Leo disagrees, and says he does not think it suits everybody. People who need structure, who dislike selling themselves, or who have a family depending on a regular salary may be much happier employed. In his opinion, the idea that everyone should be their own boss is a fashion, not a fact. Kamila admits that she had hoped for a more cheerful answer.

For listeners thinking of jumping, his advice is simple. Do not resign first. Start with one evening project a week, build a small group of clients, and leave only when freelance income has covered your salary for six months in a row. Kamila thanks him, and says the next episode will be about how to survive working from a kitchen table.

items.prompt: How long did Zafar work as a lawyer?
items.audio:
Hello, everyone. My name is Zafar Ibragimov, and the headteacher has asked me to talk about changing careers, which is a little funny, because when I was your age I told my teachers I would never change anything. I wanted to be a lawyer, and I became one. I studied law for five years, worked for a firm in Tashkent for eleven years, and for most of that time I told myself I was happy.

The first crack appeared when I was thirty seven. I was working late on a contract, and I realised that I could not remember the last time I had made anything with my hands. Not a dish, not a shelf, not even a paper aeroplane. That evening I went home and built a small stool from a pile of wood my neighbour was throwing away. It was terrible. It wobbled, it was ugly, and my wife said it looked like a table that had given up. But I was happier that night than I had been all year.

Of course, I did not quit the next day. I want to be clear about that, because many people think a career change is a dramatic moment. For me it was slow and boring. For two years I attended carpentry classes in the evenings, and I kept my job. Then I reduced my hours to four days a week, and used the fifth for a workshop that I rented from a friend. I made furniture, sold some to colleagues, and slowly learned that I enjoyed being bad at something, because it meant I was learning.

The money was difficult. In my first year as a full time carpenter I earned about a third of my lawyer's salary. My wife, who is a dentist, supported us, and I will always be grateful. I was ready to go back to law if it did not work. Fortunately, in the second year, a hotel ordered thirty chairs, and after that, orders came more regularly. Today I employ four people, two of whom are former students of this school, so I suppose that I have something in common with your teachers.

Now I must be careful, because I do not want you to leave here thinking that everyone should abandon their job and pick up a hammer. Some of my former colleagues are very happy in law, and they say that I was lucky. They are partly right. I had savings, a supportive wife and no children at the time. If I had had three children and a loan, I might not have been brave. So the lesson is not be brave. The lesson is to prepare, and to test your idea cheaply before you bet your life on it.

Also, remember that skills transfer. I use my legal training every day, when I read contracts from customers, and my patience as a lawyer is useful with clients who change their minds eight times about the colour of a cupboard.

I will finish with a question. If you were told that you could not fail, what would you try? Think about it, and then ask me anything.

items.prompt: How long does the scheme last now?
items.audio:
Good evening, parents, and good evening to the young people who have been dragged here by their parents, or perhaps it is the other way round. My name is Beatrice Owusu, and I coordinate the engineering apprenticeship scheme at the college. I am going to explain how it works, what it costs, which is nothing, and what it will not give you, which is an easy life.

An apprenticeship is a real job with a real salary and a qualification at the end. For three years you work for a company four days a week and spend the fifth day here at college. Some people believe the scheme lasts two years. That used to be the case, but the government changed the rules, so now it is three, and the third year is where you really become useful. In the first year the salary is about eleven thousand pounds, in the second year it rises to fourteen thousand, and in the third, to nineteen. I know that sounds modest, but remember that you pay no tuition fees, and that your classmates who go to university will graduate owing a great deal of money.

Who can apply? You do not need a degree, and you do not need to have studied engineering. What you do need is a pass in mathematics at the school leaving exam, and the ability to work in a team. We also give a short practical test, in which you have to assemble a small machine from instructions. Do not worry, nobody fails because they could not finish it. We are looking at how you approach the problem, whether you ask for help, and whether you stay calm when the second screw falls on the floor.

Applications open on the first of February and close on the thirtieth of March. Please be careful: that is the thirtieth, not the thirteenth, as it says in the old brochure that some of you are holding. Interviews take place in April, and the first day of work is in September. We have places for sixty students this year, and last year we received nearly four hundred applications, so I will not pretend that it is easy.

Now, what are the downsides? First, the working day is long. You start at seven thirty on the factory floor, not at the leisurely hour some students enjoy, and you will be tired. Second, you are an employee, so if you are repeatedly late or careless, the company can dismiss you, and the college cannot protect you. Third, not every company is wonderful. A few years ago, one of our partner firms used its apprentices only to sweep the floor, and we removed it from the scheme immediately. If you ever feel you are not learning anything, tell me, and I will act.

On the positive side, ninety percent of our graduates stay with the company that trained them, and many are promoted within five years. One of our first graduates is now a production manager and, I am proud to say, tells everyone that the best decision of his life was to skip university.

I have brochures on the table at the back. Please take one, and take it seriously, but check the dates.

items.prompt: How long has Dmitri worked as an accountant?
items.audio:
This is the career advice hour, and I am your host, Carla Benitez. Today's first caller is Dmitri, who has worked as an accountant for six years and wants to ask for a raise. He says he has never done it before and that his hands are sweating just thinking about it. Carla tells him that is perfectly normal, and then she gives him a plan.

Her first piece of advice is about timing. Dmitri says he was thinking of asking on Monday morning, because he wants to get it over with. Carla says that is the worst possible moment, as managers are usually busy and grumpy at the start of the week. She suggests Wednesday or Thursday, ideally after he has completed something successful. She also says never to ask on the day of a company crisis. Then she adds that, actually, the very best moment is during the annual review, if there is one, and Dmitri says there is, in November. Carla tells him to prepare in October.

Her second point is about evidence. She says that people who say I deserve more because I have been here a long time rarely succeed. Years of service are not a reason; results are. So Dmitri should write a list of what he has achieved, with numbers where possible. He mentions that he reduced the time needed to close the monthly accounts from eight days to five, and that he trained two juniors. Carla is delighted, and says that is the sort of detail that wins arguments.

The third point is the number itself. Dmitri earns forty two thousand and was planning to ask for forty four. Carla advises against that. She explains that the first number you say is an anchor, and if you start too low, you will end below it. She recommends that he research what similar accountants earn in the city, and if the average is forty eight, he should ask for fifty, so that there is room to compromise. Dmitri says he feels uncomfortable asking for so much. Carla replies that managers expect negotiation, and that many are surprised when people do not do it.

Then Dmitri asks what to do if the answer is no. Carla says no is rarely the end. She suggests asking what he would need to achieve to receive a raise in six months, and writing the answer down. If the manager cannot give money, he may be able to offer something else, such as extra holiday, a training budget or an occasional day at home. But she warns against threatening to leave unless he really means it, because managers sometimes say fine.

Dmitri thanks her and says he feels braver. Carla finishes with a gentle joke, that if the raise works, he owes the programme a cake. After the traffic news, the next caller is a woman who wants to know whether it is rude to ask about pay in an interview.

items.prompt: How long has Ewa worked on the site?
items.audio:
Morning, team. Gather round, please, and put your tea down for a minute, because this is the safety briefing, and I would like you to remember at least half of it. For the three new people, my name is Ewa Kowalczyk, I am the shift supervisor, and I have been on this site for nine years without a serious accident, which I would like to continue.

We start with the fire exits. There are four in this building, but only three are marked on the old plan you were given. The fourth, at the back near the cold store, was added last year, and the plan has not been updated, so please ignore the plan and trust the green signs. In case of a fire alarm, you do not collect your jacket, you do not finish the pallet, and you do not go back for your phone. You walk, not run, to the car park on the east side, which is the one with the blue fence. Not the west car park, because that is where the lorries turn, and I do not want to count you under a lorry.

Next, lifting. Many people believe that a back injury comes from lifting something very heavy. In fact most of our injuries come from lifting something light in a silly way, such as twisting while you pick up a box of tins. So bend your knees, keep the load close to your body, and turn with your feet, not your waist. The limit for one person is twenty five kilograms. Anything heavier needs two people or the trolley. If a box looks too heavy and you are not sure, it is not an insult to ask.

Forklift trucks. Only licensed drivers may use them. That includes a quick go just to move something three metres. I have seen a man lose his job over three metres. If you are on foot, wear the yellow jacket, never walk behind a truck that is reversing, and make eye contact with the driver before you cross. A driver who has not seen you, has not seen you, even if you are wearing the brightest jacket in the world.

Now, a change. Until last month, the first aid box was in the canteen. It is now in the office next to my desk, because several people used the bandages for craft projects. If you need help, shout, and someone will come. We have eight trained first aiders on site, but only two on the night shift, so on nights you should be extra careful.

Let me finish with a reminder about reporting. If you see a spill, a broken pallet or a wire hanging from the ceiling, tell me, even if you think it is minor. Nobody will be in trouble for reporting something. People get into trouble for hiding it. That is my one rule. Questions? No? Good. Then one last thing: if somebody has brought biscuits, I will pretend I did not see.

items.prompt: How many people does Yulduz's company employ?
items.audio:
This is the Business Hour, and tonight's guest is Yulduz Rakhimova, who started a delivery company five years ago and now employs ninety people. The presenter, Martin, begins by saying that most people assume she had a brilliant idea from the beginning. Yulduz laughs and says that nothing could be further from the truth.

Her original plan, she explains, was to deliver flowers. She noticed that people in her city forgot birthdays constantly, and she imagined a service that would send a bouquet within two hours. She and her brother borrowed a small sum from their uncle, bought a second hand van, and opened for business on the eighth of March, which she chose because it is a day when everyone buys flowers. Martin asks how it went. Yulduz says that the first day was spectacular, with almost two hundred orders, and the second day was empty, because flowers sell only when there is a holiday. By the end of the second month they were close to bankruptcy.

The turning point came by accident. A pharmacist next to her flower stand asked if the van could take medicine to an elderly customer who could not walk to the shop. Yulduz agreed, as a favour. A week later, three more pharmacies asked, and she realised that medicine, unlike flowers, is needed every day of the year. So she kept the flower business as a small side service, and rebuilt the whole company around pharmacies. Martin comments that this must have been scary. She says it was, but that staying with a failing idea was scarier.

Martin then asks about mistakes. Yulduz says that her biggest was hiring friends. At one point, a third of her staff were people she knew from school, and when she had to dismiss one, the friendship ended. She does not regret hiring them, but she would now be much more careful about writing clear job descriptions and agreeing expectations from the start. She also says she grew too fast: in her third year she opened offices in two other cities within a single month, and one of them lost money for eighteen months before she closed it.

When asked about advice, Yulduz refuses to say that people should follow their passion. She thinks that passion is overrated, and that the better question is, which problem do people already pay to solve? She also thinks beginners worry too much about copying, as nearly everything has been tried somewhere, and what matters is carrying it out better and more reliably.

Martin asks what the future holds. Yulduz hopes to start delivering groceries to villages that have no shops, but she says she will only do it if the numbers work, and for now it is a trial in one district. Martin thanks her, and says that after the break we will hear from a baker who sells bread only at night.

The presenter, Martin, begins by saying that most people assume she had a brilliant idea from the beginning. Yulduz laughs and says that nothing could be further from the truth.

Her original plan, she explains, was to deliver flowers. She noticed that people in her city forgot birthdays constantly, and she imagined a service that would send a bouquet within two hours. She and her brother borrowed a small sum from their uncle, bought a second hand van, and opened for business on the eighth of March, which she chose because it is a day when everyone buys flowers. Martin asks how it went. Yulduz says that the first day was spectacular, with almost two hundred orders, and the second day was empty, because flowers sell only when there is a holiday. By the end of the second month they were close to bankruptcy.

The turning point came by accident. A pharmacist next to her flower stand asked if the van could take medicine to an elderly customer who could not walk to the shop. Yulduz agreed, as a favour. A week later, three more pharmacies asked, and she realised that medicine, unlike flowers, is needed every day of the year. So she kept the flower business as a small side service, and rebuilt the whole company around pharmacies. Martin comments that this must have been scary. She says it was, but that staying with a failing idea was scarier.

Martin then asks about mistakes. Yulduz says that her biggest was hiring friends. At one point, a third of her staff were people she knew from school, and when she had to dismiss one, the friendship ended. She does not regret hiring them, but she would now be much more careful about writing clear job descriptions and agreeing expectations from the start. She also says she grew too fast: in her third year she opened offices in two other cities within a single month, and one of them lost money for eighteen months before she closed it.

When asked about advice, Yulduz refuses to say that people should follow their passion. She thinks that passion is overrated, and that the better question is, which problem do people already pay to solve? She also thinks beginners worry too much about copying, as nearly everything has been tried somewhere, and what matters is carrying it out better and more reliably.

Martin asks what the future holds. Yulduz hopes to start delivering groceries to villages that have no shops, but she says she will only do it if the numbers work, and for now it is a trial in one district. Martin thanks her, and says that after the break we will hear from a baker who sells bread only at night.

items.prompt: What is Bobur's cholesterol level this time?
items.audio:
Doctor Nilufar Karimova calls her patient Bobur Rashidov on a Monday morning to discuss the results of his blood test. She begins by saying that most of the numbers are perfectly normal, which Bobur is relieved to hear. However, his cholesterol is higher than she would like. It is six point two, she says, and then corrects herself, because that was the figure from last year. This time it is five point eight, which is still above the healthy limit but much better than before. Bobur admits that he has been eating fewer fried foods since spring, but he has not managed to take any regular exercise because of his night shifts at the bakery.

The doctor does not suggest medicine at this stage. Instead she recommends a thirty minute walk every day, preferably in the morning, although she says that a walk after supper would also be acceptable if mornings are impossible. Bobur asks whether he should give up eggs completely. She laughs and says that this is a common mistake. Eggs are fine, two or three a week, but he should avoid butter and the sausages he mentioned earlier. She also reminds him that he does not need to stop drinking coffee, only to stop adding three spoonfuls of sugar to each cup.

Then comes the part Bobur likes less. The doctor wants to see him again in the clinic for a second test. At first she proposes Thursday at fourteen hundred hours, but Bobur explains that he starts work at fifteen hundred and the bus takes an hour. She checks her calendar and says that Friday is better, at ten past nine in the morning. He must not eat anything for twelve hours before the test, but he may drink water. Bobur worries that he will faint without breakfast, so she suggests bringing a banana to eat immediately afterwards.

Before they finish, the doctor asks about his father, because heart problems often run in families. Bobur says his father had a mild heart attack at fifty, but he has been healthy ever since. Doctor Karimova says this is useful information and adds a note to the file. She also gives him her direct number, which is not the number of the clinic reception, in case he feels pain in his chest. She stresses that he should call an ambulance rather than ring her if the pain is severe. Bobur thanks her, saying he had expected much worse news, and promises to start walking on Tuesday, not Monday, because he will be too tired after the night shift today.

items.prompt: What is the professor's current opinion about the eight hour rule?
items.audio:
Good evening and welcome to Healthy Habits. Tonight my guest is Professor Dilshod Yusupov, who has studied sleep for more than twenty years. Professor, many of our listeners believe that everyone needs exactly eight hours. Is that true? The professor smiles and says that he used to repeat that rule himself, but he no longer does. Most adults need between seven and nine hours, and what matters even more is going to bed and getting up at roughly the same time every day, including weekends. A person who sleeps eight hours but changes the schedule by three hours at the weekend often feels worse than someone who sleeps seven hours regularly.

The presenter then asks about teenagers. The professor explains that their body clock moves later during puberty, so a sixteen year old who cannot fall asleep before midnight is not being lazy. He believes schools should start later, and he says that in one town where lessons began at half past eight instead of eight, the number of students who fell asleep in class dropped by almost a third. He admits, however, that this idea is unpopular with many parents, who worry about their working hours.

Next come naps. Many listeners have written to ask whether a long afternoon sleep is harmful. The professor says that a short nap of about twenty minutes can improve concentration, but a nap of an hour or more may leave you feeling heavy and can make it harder to sleep at night. The exception is people who work night shifts, for whom a longer nap before work can be very helpful.

Then he turns to the bedroom. The ideal temperature is around eighteen degrees, he says, much cooler than most people think. He also recommends switching off screens an hour before bed. When the presenter says that she reads the news on her phone in the dark, the professor shakes his head, although he accepts that a strict ban is unrealistic. Coffee is another topic. He advises avoiding it for at least six hours before bedtime, because its effect lasts much longer than people imagine. One surprising point is that alcohol, which many people use to relax, actually makes sleep lighter and more broken.

Finally, the presenter asks for one piece of advice for tired listeners. The professor answers that they should not try to fix everything at once. Choose one change, he says, such as a fixed wake up time, and keep it for two weeks before adding another. The presenter thanks him and says she will begin with that, and that her phone will now stay in the kitchen.
options: Six hours is enough for adults

Professor, many of our listeners believe that everyone needs exactly eight hours. Is that true? The professor smiles and says that he used to repeat that rule himself, but he no longer does. Most adults need between seven and nine hours, and what matters even more is going to bed and getting up at roughly the same time every day, including weekends. A person who sleeps eight hours but changes the schedule by three hours at the weekend often feels worse than someone who sleeps seven hours regularly.

The presenter then asks about teenagers. The professor explains that their body clock moves later during puberty, so a sixteen year old who cannot fall asleep before midnight is not being lazy. He believes schools should start later, and he says that in one town where lessons began at half past eight instead of eight, the number of students who fell asleep in class dropped by almost a third. He admits, however, that this idea is unpopular with many parents, who worry about their working hours.

Next come naps. Many listeners have written to ask whether a long afternoon sleep is harmful. The professor says that a short nap of about twenty minutes can improve concentration, but a nap of an hour or more may leave you feeling heavy and can make it harder to sleep at night. The exception is people who work night shifts, for whom a longer nap before work can be very helpful.

Then he turns to the bedroom. The ideal temperature is around eighteen degrees, he says, much cooler than most people think. He also recommends switching off screens an hour before bed. When the presenter says that she reads the news on her phone in the dark, the professor shakes his head, although he accepts that a strict ban is unrealistic. Coffee is another topic. He advises avoiding it for at least six hours before bedtime, because its effect lasts much longer than people imagine. One surprising point is that alcohol, which many people use to relax, actually makes sleep lighter and more broken.

Finally, the presenter asks for one piece of advice for tired listeners. The professor answers that they should not try to fix everything at once. Choose one change, he says, such as a fixed wake up time, and keep it for two weeks before adding another. The presenter thanks him and says she will begin with that, and that her phone will now stay in the kitchen.

items.prompt: When does the club open at weekends?
items.audio:
Malika works at the front desk of the Olympus Fitness Club, and this morning she is showing a new visitor, James, around the building. She begins at the reception and explains that the club is open from six in the morning until eleven at night on weekdays, but only from eight until eight at the weekend. James says he is thinking of training before work, so the early opening suits him perfectly.

The first room is the main gym, which has about sixty machines and a large area for free weights. Malika warns him that it is extremely crowded between five and seven in the evening, when most people finish work. If he wants a quiet session, she suggests coming around noon, when the room is almost empty. She adds that every new member receives a free introduction with a trainer, which lasts forty minutes and is not compulsory, but she strongly recommends it, especially for beginners who might hurt their backs by lifting too much.

Next they walk past the studio where the classes take place. Yoga begins at half past seven every morning, and spinning classes are on Tuesday and Thursday evenings. James says he has never tried yoga and doubts it is for him, but Malika tells him that many of the strongest men in the club attend, and that he can try the first class for nothing.

Then they reach the swimming pool. It is twenty five metres long and heated all year round. Malika points out that the pool is closed every Wednesday for cleaning, not on Tuesdays as many visitors expect, so he should not plan a swim that day. Changing rooms are downstairs, and the lockers work with a coin or with your own padlock. A coin is returned when you open the locker, so nobody loses money. Towels are not included, but they can be rented for a small fee.

Back at the desk, Malika explains the prices. A monthly membership costs thirty five dollars, whereas the yearly one costs three hundred, which works out much cheaper. There is also a joining fee of fifteen dollars, which the club sometimes waives in September. James first says that he will take the yearly option, but then he hesitates, because he is moving to another city in the spring. In the end he chooses the monthly plan, so that he can leave without losing money. Malika gives him a card, shows him the entrance code, and tells him to bring a water bottle tomorrow, because the machines near the window have no cooler.

items.prompt: What does the doctor say about breakfast?
items.answer: It matters less than the quality of the whole day's food
items.audio:
In today's programme the host, Aziza, interviews the nutritionist Doctor Gulnora Sattarova about common myths on healthy eating. Aziza starts with breakfast, which people often call the most important meal of the day. The doctor says that this is only partly true. Some people feel full of energy without eating anything until noon, and for them forcing a big breakfast makes little sense. What counts is the total quality of food during the day. She admits that ten years ago she would have told every patient to eat five small meals, but the research has changed, and now she says that three proper meals and perhaps one snack work well for most people.

Aziza then asks about sugar. Doctor Sattarova explains that the recommended limit for an adult is about fifty grams of added sugar a day, and she stresses that this is a maximum, not a target. Many people are shocked to learn that a single glass of fruit juice from a shop may contain nearly all of that. She adds that fresh fruit is quite different, because the fibre slows down the way the body absorbs sugar. Aziza says she has always thought juice was healthier than lemonade, and the doctor replies that it is slightly better but not by as much as advertisements suggest.

The conversation moves to bread and rice. Many of the doctor's patients are afraid of carbohydrates and want to cut them out completely. She disagrees. Whole grain bread, rice and potatoes give energy and are not harmful in sensible amounts. The real problem is white flour products such as pastries, which are eaten in large quantities. She also recommends at least five portions of vegetables and fruit daily, although she points out that potatoes do not count as one of the five.

Aziza asks about vitamins. Doctor Sattarova believes that most healthy people do not need expensive supplements, with one exception. In winter, when there is little sunshine, vitamin D tablets are useful, and she takes them herself from October until March. As for fasting, which has become fashionable, she was sceptical at first, but after reading several studies she now says that it can help some people, although it is not suitable for pregnant women or for anyone who has diabetes.

At the end, Aziza asks for one simple rule. The doctor says it is to cook at home at least four evenings a week, because when you prepare food yourself you control the salt, the oil and the portions. Aziza laughs and says she will try, although she cooks only twice a week at present.
options: It matters less than the quality of the whole day's food
It should be skipped by everyone

items.prompt: Why does Olga refuse to sell Sanjar antibiotics?
items.answer: He has no prescription and has a virus
items.audio:
Sanjar walks into a pharmacy on a cold Tuesday afternoon, coughing and holding a tissue. The pharmacist, Miss Olga Petrova, asks how she can help. Sanjar says that he has had a sore throat and a blocked nose for five days, and that last night he also had a slight fever. He would like some antibiotics, because the last time he took them he felt better very quickly. Olga explains politely that she cannot sell antibiotics without a prescription, and that in any case they do not work against colds, which are caused by viruses. Sanjar looks disappointed, but he admits that his sister, who is a nurse, told him the same thing.

Olga suggests a different treatment. She recommends tablets that reduce fever and relieve a sore throat, and a spray for the nose. The tablets must be taken one every eight hours, never more than three in a day, and always after food, because they can irritate the stomach. Sanjar asks whether he can drink a glass of wine at the weekend. She tells him firmly that he must not drink any alcohol while he is taking them. The spray, she adds, should be used for no more than five days, otherwise the nose may become blocked again, which surprises Sanjar.

Then Olga asks whether he has any allergies. Sanjar says that he is allergic to penicillin, and she says that this is very important and notes it on the screen. She also asks if he drives to work. He says that he drives a delivery van. She warns that some cold remedies make people sleepy, but this brand does not, so there is no problem. Another brand, which is cheaper, does cause drowsiness, so she does not recommend it for him.

Before he pays, Sanjar remembers that his daughter, who is six, has started coughing too. He asks for something for her. Olga says that children need a different medicine, a syrup, and explains that the dose is five millilitres, twice a day, using the small measuring spoon in the box, not an ordinary kitchen spoon. She says that if the cough lasts more than a week, or if the girl has difficulty breathing, he should take her to a doctor immediately.

The total comes to forty thousand sums for the adult tablets and the spray, and twenty thousand more for the syrup. Sanjar pays and says that he wanted to buy a vitamin product as well but decides against it because of the price. Olga says that this is sensible, since good food and rest will help him more. She wishes him a quick recovery and reminds him to come back if he is not better by Sunday.
options: He has no prescription and has a virus

items.prompt: How many weeks are left before the race?
items.audio:
Good evening, everybody, and welcome to the final information meeting for our club's marathon group. My name is Aziz, and I have been coaching runners for eleven years. The race takes place on the fourteenth of October, which is exactly twelve weeks from today, and tonight I want to explain the training plan and the mistakes I see every year.

The plan is simple. You will run four times a week, and one of those runs is a long one on Sunday morning. We start with ten kilometres and add a little each week, but never more than ten percent. Last year a man in our group added too much too quickly and had to stop with a sore knee in week six. The longest run will be thirty two kilometres, three weeks before the race. Some people ask why we do not run the full forty two kilometres in training. The answer is that your body needs time to recover, and the damage from such a long run would cost you more than it gives you.

Now, a change from what I told some of you in the spring. At that time I recommended eating huge plates of pasta the night before the race. I have changed my mind. Research suggests that you should increase your carbohydrates over the last three days, not just in one meal, and you should avoid anything new or heavy. On race morning, have breakfast three hours before the start. The race begins at half past seven, so that means your alarm should ring at four thirty, which I know sounds terrible.

Let me talk about equipment. Buy your shoes at least a month before the race and wear them in training. The worst thing you can do is to put on brand new shoes at the start line, because you will almost certainly get blisters. The same applies to clothes. Do not try a new shirt on race day.

On pace, beginners usually start far too fast because of the crowd and the excitement. Please run the first five kilometres slower than your target speed. If your goal is five hours, which is realistic for most of you, you should average about seven minutes per kilometre. If you feel tired, there is no shame in walking for one minute at each water station. The only people who must not walk are those aiming for under four hours, but I do not think anyone in this room is in that group.

Finally, the last week. Run only twice, very gently, and take Friday as a complete rest day. Sleep is more important than any workout now. Questions? Yes, the lady in the green jacket, please.

items.prompt: How long has Kamila had the pain?
items.audio:
Kamila has been putting off this appointment for almost a year, and as she sits in the waiting room she wishes she had never made it. Eventually the dentist, Doctor Evans, invites her in and asks what the problem is. Kamila explains that she has had a pain in a tooth at the bottom on the left side for about three weeks. It hurts mainly when she drinks something cold, but yesterday it also hurt when she had hot tea. At first she thought it would pass, which she now admits was a mistake.

Doctor Evans examines the tooth and takes an X-ray. After a few minutes he explains that there is a large hole, a cavity, that has reached quite deep into the tooth. The good news is that he can save it. Kamila had been afraid that it would have to be taken out, but a filling will be enough, and he does not think a root treatment is necessary, although he says that if she had waited another month, it might have been. Kamila feels a mixture of relief and embarrassment.

The dentist then talks about the procedure. He will give her an injection to numb the area, which will last about two hours, so she should not eat or drink anything hot until it wears off, otherwise she might burn her tongue without noticing. The filling itself takes about twenty minutes. Kamila asks whether it will hurt, and he promises that she will feel only a little pressure. She says she has always been terrified of the sound of the drill, and he kindly offers her headphones with music, which she gratefully accepts.

While he works, Doctor Evans chats about her teeth in general. He notices that her gums are slightly red and asks how often she cleans between her teeth. Kamila says she brushes twice a day but never uses floss. He says that is the cause of the redness, and that without change she might develop gum disease in a few years. He recommends floss or small brushes once a day. Kamila asks whether an electric toothbrush would be better. He says it is helpful but not necessary, and that technique matters more than the price of the brush.

At the end, the receptionist tells her that the treatment costs one hundred and fifty dollars, which is covered partly by her insurance, so she pays only sixty. Doctor Evans asks her to return in six months for a check, not in a year, as she did this time. Kamila promises that she will, and she leaves feeling much braver than she expected, even though her mouth feels strange and her lip is still numb.

items.prompt: When did Hans Selye first describe stress?
items.audio:
Good morning, everyone. Today's lecture is about stress, a word we all use but rarely define. Let me begin with a surprise. Stress is not always bad. The scientist Hans Selye, who first described it in the nineteen thirties, argued that a little stress helps us perform. Before an exam or a job interview, your heart beats faster and your attention sharpens. That is acute stress, and it usually disappears when the situation ends. The real danger is chronic stress, which continues for weeks and months, for example because of an unhappy job or financial worries.

To show how serious this can be, I want to describe a study that followed four hundred office workers for five years. The researchers found that those who reported constant pressure were nearly twice as likely to develop high blood pressure. I should add that the study had a weakness: most participants were men over forty, so we cannot be certain that the same results would apply to young women. A second finding was interesting. It was not the amount of work that caused the most harm, but the feeling of having no control. Workers who could decide how to organise their day suffered less, even if they worked longer hours.

So what can we do? I will mention three things. The first is physical activity. Even a brisk walk of twenty minutes lowers the level of stress hormones. The second is sleep. People who sleep badly react to small problems as if they were disasters. The third is breathing. A simple exercise is to breathe in for four seconds, hold for seven, and breathe out for eight. Some of my students laughed when I first suggested it, but those who tried it said it worked.

Now I would like to express an opinion that not everyone in my field shares. Many apps promise to remove stress with five minute meditations. In my view they are oversold. I have no objection to them, and some people clearly benefit, but they cannot replace the deeper causes, such as a heavy workload or lack of social contact. Spending time with friends, in my experience, is far more effective than any app. I was sceptical about this myself, but the data are consistent.

Before the break, I should mention what stress is not. It is not a sign of weakness, and it is not something you can simply decide not to feel. After the break we will look at stress in students, and next week there will be a short test on today's material. Please read chapter six before then, and do not leave it until the last night, as many of you did last time.

items.prompt: What dish is Chef Rustam cooking?
items.audio:
Hello and welcome back to Fresh and Simple, the show where we prove that healthy food does not have to be boring. I am your host, Chef Rustam, and today we are going to make a dish that I have cooked for my own family for years, baked chickpeas with spinach and lemon yoghurt. It is cheap, it is full of protein, and best of all, you can have it on the table in less than an hour.

When I planned this episode, I originally wanted to fry the chickpeas in a lot of oil, because that gives a lovely crunchy taste. But our producer, Nargiza, reminded me that this is a healthy eating programme, so I changed my mind. We are going to bake them instead. I must admit that the result is just as good, and some viewers who tried the baked version told me they prefer it. Honesty is important, so I will also say that it is not exactly the same as the fried version, but it is close enough.

Let me list what we need for four servings. Two tins of chickpeas, or about three hundred grams if you cook them yourself from dry. A big bunch of fresh spinach, one onion, two cloves of garlic, one lemon, a small cup of plain yoghurt, and a teaspoon each of cumin and paprika. Notice that there is no cream in the recipe. Many people ask me to add cream to the sauce, but yoghurt does the same job with far fewer calories. And please note, we are adding no salt at the beginning. Chickpeas from a tin already contain some, so you should taste at the end.

The preparation takes about fifteen minutes. You wash and dry the chickpeas, and that is important, because wet chickpeas will never become crisp. Then you toss them with a spoonful of olive oil and the spices, and spread them on a tray. They go into the oven at two hundred degrees for forty minutes. Meanwhile, you cook the onion and garlic gently in a pan, add the spinach, and wait until it has shrunk. Do not cook it too long, or it will turn grey and lose its vitamins.

A tip from my grandmother, who taught me everything: squeeze the lemon juice at the very end, never before, because the acid dulls the green colour. And do not worry if your kitchen is small, or if you have only one pan. We will manage. Now, wash your hands, put on your apron, and let us begin. If you have a question, send us a message after the show, and I will answer the most interesting one next week.

items.prompt: What are the nurse's new office hours?
items.audio:
Good morning, students and teachers. This is Mrs Hamidova, your school nurse, with several important announcements for this week. Please listen carefully, because some of this information concerns your parents too, and I will not repeat it tomorrow.

First, a change of hours. Until now my office has been open from nine until three, but starting Monday I will be available from eight until two. This is because the clinic has asked me to attend a training course every afternoon for a month. If you have an emergency after two, please go to the main office, where the secretary will phone for help. For small problems, such as a headache or a scratch, try to come during break time and not in the middle of a lesson.

Second, I must tell you about a problem in grade five. Three children there have been found with head lice. This is not a reason for shame, because it happens in every school, and it has nothing to do with being clean. However, it spreads quickly. Parents of grade five students will receive a letter today, and I ask them to check their children's hair this evening. Children who have lice should stay at home until they have been treated, but they do not need to stay away for a whole week. One day is usually enough. Please do not share combs, hats or hair ribbons with friends.

Third, the flu vaccination. It will be given on Wednesday the twentieth, not Thursday, as the first notice mistakenly said. It is free for all students, but only if your parents sign the permission form. The forms must be returned to your class teacher by Friday of this week. Without the form, I cannot give the injection, even if you ask me politely. Students who are ill on Wednesday will be vaccinated at a later date.

Fourth, a reminder about illness. If you have a temperature higher than thirty eight degrees, you must stay at home and return only after you have been free of fever for twenty four hours. I know that some of you would rather come to school, especially before a test, but you may infect other pupils. Students with asthma should always carry their inhalers, and I will keep a spare one in my office, in the white cupboard.

Lastly, our cafeteria has stopped selling food containing peanuts because two students are severely allergic. Please do not bring peanut butter sandwiches. Thank you for your cooperation, and remember, if you do not feel well, come and see me. That is what I am here for.

items.prompt: How did Ravshan hurt his knee?
items.audio:
Ravshan arrives for his third session at the physiotherapy centre, limping slightly, and his therapist, Miss Clarke, asks how the week has gone. Ravshan injured his knee two weeks ago while playing football with his colleagues, and he is desperate to play again because the company tournament is in a month. He says that the knee feels better, but when he went down the stairs yesterday it hurt more than he expected.

Miss Clarke asks him to lie on the bench and gently bends the knee. She explains that the swelling has gone down a lot, which is an excellent sign, but that the ligament is still weak. Ravshan asks if he will be able to take part in the tournament. She says honestly that she does not think so. He hoped to be back in four weeks, but she believes six is more realistic, and even then he should start with light training. Ravshan sighs, then says that he would rather miss one tournament than hurt his knee permanently.

They go through the exercises. Miss Clarke gives him a new set to do at home, three times a day. He should lie on his back and lift the straight leg slowly twenty times, then do ten gentle squats with his back against the wall. She emphasises that pain is a signal and he must stop immediately if it becomes sharp, although a mild ache is normal. Ravshan says that his previous therapist told him to do the exercises until he felt it burn, but Miss Clarke disagrees, saying that this is bad advice for this kind of injury.

She then talks about ice and heat. For the first days, ice was best, but now that the swelling is almost gone, he can use a warm towel for ten minutes before the exercises to loosen the muscles, and ice for twenty minutes afterwards. Ravshan asks about swimming, since his friends said it would be good for him. She agrees that swimming is excellent, but not breaststroke, because the kicking movement twists the knee. Front crawl or simply walking in the water is fine.

Before he leaves, she gives him a card with his next appointment on Thursday at five thirty, and reminds him to wear loose trousers, because last time she had trouble reaching the knee. She also suggests that he comes to watch the tournament and enjoy it as a supporter. Ravshan laughs and says that this will be painful in another way, but he promises to think about it.
