First, a change of plan. The weather forecast for tomorrow afternoon is bad, with storms expected after two o'clock. That is why we will start at six in the morning, not at seven as in the programme, and we will reach the lake before noon. If the sky looks dark, we will turn back, and I do not want any arguments about that.

Now, first aid. The most common problem on this route is blisters. They appear when your feet are wet or when your boots do not fit. If you feel a hot spot on your heel, stop immediately and cover it with a plaster. Do not wait until it becomes painful, because then it is too late. Do not burst a blister either, unless it is very large, and if it does burst, clean it carefully and cover it again.

The second problem is dehydration. In the mountain air, you lose water without noticing. Each person should carry at least two litres for the day, and more if it is hot. Do not wait until you are thirsty. Signs of dehydration are a headache, dizziness and very dark urine, which I mention only because it is a reliable sign. If someone in the group has these symptoms, tell me at once. Drinking a lot of water in one go is not the answer, and it is better to take small sips.

Then, sprained ankles. If someone falls and twists an ankle, we stop, remove the boot only if the foot is not swollen, and tie a firm bandage around it. Never walk on a badly sprained ankle just to prove you are tough. I carry a small radio, and there is a rescue post at the lake. There is no phone signal after the second bridge, so the radio is our only link.

Some of you are worried about snakes. You will probably not see any, because they avoid people. If somebody is bitten, which is extremely rare, the person should sit still and stay calm. Do not cut the wound, and do not try to suck out the poison, which is a myth from films. We keep the arm or leg below the level of the heart and call for help. The emergency number is on the card I am handing out now.

One final point. Everybody must tell me if they take regular medication, such as for asthma or diabetes. Please do that privately, if you prefer, before we start walking. Thank you, and now let us enjoy the mountains.

items.prompt: How many times a day did Zarina unlock her phone?
items.audio:
Welcome to Slow Living, the podcast about doing less and enjoying it more. I am Zarina, and this week I did something I had been afraid of for years. I spent an entire weekend without my smartphone. I want to tell you how it went, and then talk to a psychologist about why it is so difficult.

Let me start with a surprising number. Before the experiment I installed a small program that counts how often I unlock my phone. I expected about thirty times a day. The real figure was ninety six. That means that, in a waking day of sixteen hours, I picked up my phone roughly every ten minutes. I felt a little ashamed, to be honest, and a little relieved that I was not trying to lie to myself.

On Friday evening I put the phone into a drawer and gave my sister the key. I predicted that I would panic about missing messages from work. In fact, the first few hours were uncomfortable, but not for that reason. What I missed was the habit. My hand kept reaching for my pocket when I was waiting for the kettle. On Saturday morning I took a long walk, and for the first time in months I noticed the trees, the smell of bread from the bakery, and an old man feeding pigeons. By the afternoon, I read a whole book chapter without stopping, which I had not done for ages.

Now I must be fair. It was not entirely wonderful. On Saturday evening I wanted to check the address of a restaurant where I was meeting friends, and I had no way of doing it. I had to borrow my neighbour's phone, and that felt like cheating. So I cannot honestly say that I lived completely without technology, and I would not recommend such a total ban for everyone. People who care for sick relatives, for example, need to be reachable.

My guest today is the psychologist Doctor Anvar Nurmatov. He says that the main problem is not time spent on the phone but the way it breaks our attention. Each notification, even if we ignore it, takes our mind away from what we are doing, and it takes about twenty minutes to return to full concentration. His advice is not to give up the phone but to make small rules. Keep it out of the bedroom, turn off all notifications except calls, and have one hour every evening without screens. He tried the hour rule himself and, he says, he sleeps far better.

As for me, after the weekend I decided to keep two of his rules. The phone now charges in the kitchen, and the hour before bed belongs to books. Notifications, I admit, are still on, but I am working on that.

items.prompt: Why does Dana want to go on the retreat?
items.answer: Her doctor advised her to rest
items.audio:
Dana phones the reception of the Silver Valley Yoga Retreat on a Sunday evening, and a cheerful receptionist named Leyla answers. Dana explains that she wants to book a week in the mountains because she has been working long hours and her doctor has advised her to rest. Leyla says that the retreat offers seven night programmes, starting every second Saturday from April until October.

Dana first asks about June. Leyla checks the calendar and says that the programme beginning on the seventh of June still has places. Dana hesitates, because her manager has not yet approved her holiday, and she says that the end of the summer would be better. After a short pause, she changes her mind again, saying that September would be quieter at work, and asks whether the programme on the twelfth of September is available. Leyla says that it is, but only two places are left, so Dana should decide quickly.

Then they talk about accommodation. A single room costs nine hundred dollars for the week, and a shared room costs six hundred and fifty per person. Dana prefers privacy, but the price is high, so she asks for the shared room, and she would be happy to be matched with a quiet person. Leyla promises to check with the other guests and notes that the shared rooms have two beds and a small balcony with a view of the valley.

Dana is vegetarian and asks about the food. Leyla says that all meals are vegetarian, with the exception of Saturday dinner, when fish is served, but guests can always ask for an alternative. Breakfast is at half past seven, after the morning yoga session, which starts at six. There is no coffee, only herbal tea, and Dana laughs and says that she will manage, though she suspects the first two days will be hard. Phones are allowed in the rooms but not in the yoga hall.

Finally, Dana asks about cancellation. Leyla explains the rules carefully. If Dana cancels more than thirty days before the start, she gets a full refund. Between thirty and fifteen days before, she gets fifty percent back, and if she cancels later than that, there is no refund at all. Dana says that this seems fair. To keep the room she must pay a deposit of two hundred dollars within three days. Dana says she will do it tomorrow morning by card, and Leyla sends her an email with all the details and the booking number. Dana thanks her and says she is already looking forward to the quiet.
options: Her doctor advised her to rest

items.prompt: Where will the donation take place?
items.audio:
Good afternoon, everyone. My name is Feruza Alimova, and I am a volunteer coordinator for the city blood service. Thank you for staying a few minutes after the lecture. I want to tell you about our donation day, which will take place next Thursday at the university, and I hope to persuade some of you to take part.

First, a change. In the posters you may have seen that the donation was planned in the library, but because of repairs, it has been moved to the sports hall, on the ground floor beside the swimming pool. The hours are from nine in the morning until four in the afternoon, and there is no need to make an appointment, although it helps us if you register online to avoid long queues, especially around noon.

Who can donate? You must be at least eighteen years old and weigh at least fifty kilograms. You should feel healthy on the day, so if you have a cold or a fever, please wait until you have recovered for two weeks. There are some other restrictions that people often do not know. If you have had a tattoo or a piercing in the last six months, you cannot give blood. If you have taken antibiotics, you must wait until the course is finished and then one more week. People who have travelled to certain tropical countries recently may also be asked to wait. The nurses will ask you questions in private, so please be completely honest. Everything is confidential.

Some students worry that giving blood is painful or dangerous. In reality, the needle is felt for only a few seconds. The actual donation takes about ten minutes, but the whole visit, including the questions, the check and the rest afterwards, takes about an hour. We take around four hundred and fifty millilitres, which your body replaces within a few weeks. Men can donate every three months, and women every four, because they lose iron more quickly. This is a difference that surprises many people.

Please eat a good meal before you come, and drink plenty of water. Do not come on an empty stomach, as this is the main reason why people feel dizzy. Avoid fatty food, for example fried meat, because it makes the blood plasma cloudy and difficult to use. After donating, you will receive a snack and a voucher for a free lunch at the university cafeteria. You should not do heavy exercise for the rest of the day, so I would not play football in the evening.

One donation can help up to three people, which is a good reason to take ten minutes. Hospitals in our city are always short of blood, especially in summer. If you have questions, find me at the table outside or write to the address on the screen.

items.prompt: When does the connection usually fail?
items.audio:
Dilnoza calls the help line of her internet provider at ten past nine on a Monday morning because her connection has been dropping for three days. The agent, a patient man called Martin, asks her to describe the problem. She explains that the wireless signal disappears every evening around seven, just when her children want to watch their cartoons. At first she says the router is the white box in the hall, but then she corrects herself and says it is actually the black one on the bookshelf, because the white box is only a telephone socket.

Martin asks her to unplug the router for thirty seconds and plug it in again. Dilnoza complains that she has already done that twice and that nothing changed. Martin says he understands, but he must follow the checklist before he can send an engineer. While the router restarts, he asks which lights are on. She reports that the power light is green, the wireless light is green, and the internet light is orange. Martin explains that an orange internet light usually means the problem is outside the house, not inside it, so she does not need to buy a new router, which is exactly what her neighbour had advised her to do last week.

Next Martin checks the line from his office and sees a fault on the cable in her street. He says an engineer could come on Wednesday between one and three in the afternoon. Dilnoza sighs, because she works on Wednesday afternoons, and she asks whether Thursday morning is possible. items.prompt: Why was the first observation delayed until October?
items.audio:
Good morning, and welcome to the science bulletin. Our main story today comes from the Atacama Desert in Chile, where astronomers have finally switched on the Aurora Array, a telescope that has taken eleven years to build. The project was supposed to be ready last March, but a series of dust storms and a strike by truck drivers pushed the first observation back to October. Professor Aigerim Nurlanova, who leads the international team, told our reporter that she had almost given up hope of meeting even the new deadline.

The Aurora Array is not the biggest telescope in the world, a title that still belongs to a competing project in Hawaii, but its supporters argue that size is not everything. Instead of one enormous mirror, it uses fifty-five smaller mirrors that work together as a single eye. This design, according to the professor, makes the images sharper and the whole system cheaper to repair, because a damaged mirror can be replaced in a week without stopping the observations. The total cost was just under two billion dollars, which she admits is a great deal of money, although she insists it is less than the original estimate.

The first target of the telescope will be a star about fourteen light years from Earth, which is known to have at least two planets. The team hopes to find out whether either of them has an atmosphere containing water vapour. Professor Nurlanova was careful not to promise too much. She said that a result of that kind would take months of careful analysis, and that anyone expecting a sensational announcement by the end of the year would be disappointed.

Not everyone is celebrating. Several families who live in the nearest village, about forty kilometres away, complain that the observatory uses a large amount of water in a region where rain is rare. A spokesman for the project replied that most of the water is recycled and that the observatory has paid for a new well that will also serve the village. Our reporter, however, noticed that several villagers were still not convinced, and one farmer said he would wait to see the well working before he changed his mind.

Despite these doubts, the mood at the site on opening night was cheerful. About two hundred guests watched the first image appear on a screen, and when it did, the professor, who rarely shows her feelings, wiped her eyes. The first public pictures will be released next Friday. And now, the weather.
options: A fault in the main mirror

items.prompt: How long has Rustam worked in computer security?
items.audio:
Thank you all for coming this evening. My name is Rustam Karimov, and I have worked in computer security for fourteen years. Tonight I want to change the way you think about passwords, because most of the advice you have been given is, frankly, out of date. For years we were told to choose a short password full of strange symbols and to change it every ninety days. Today almost every expert, including me, thinks that was a mistake. When people are forced to change passwords all the time, they simply add a number at the end, so that Summer one becomes Summer two, and a thief can guess that in seconds.

What works much better is length. A password of sixteen characters made from four ordinary words, for example the name of a fruit, a street, a colour and a piece of furniture, is far harder to break than a short password with clever symbols. Notice that I said sixteen, not sixty. Nobody needs to type sixty characters, and the extra effort would not make you any safer. The words should be unrelated, though. A phrase from a famous song is not a good choice, because attackers try those first.

The second rule is never to use the same password twice. Last year a large shopping website lost the details of about eight million customers, and I mean eight, not eighty, although that was still a disaster. Within a day, criminals tried the same email addresses and passwords on banks and social networks. People who had used one password everywhere lost money, while those with different passwords were fine. Of course, nobody can remember forty different phrases, so I recommend a password manager. I know some of you distrust them, and I used to be one of those people, but I changed my mind after I saw how many accounts my own family had lost.

The third rule is to switch on two-step verification wherever you can. This sends a code to your phone, and without it a thief cannot enter your account even if he knows your password. The only exception I would make is for services that hold nothing important, such as a forum you visit once a year. For your email, your bank and your social media, there is no excuse.

Finally, a word about being careful with messages. No bank will ever ask you for your password by telephone or by email. If a message makes you feel panic, stop, close it and contact the company directly. In my experience, the people who lose most are not the ones with weak technology but the ones who hurry. Now, please ask me anything you like, and I promise to answer honestly.

items.prompt: According to Rustam, the people who lose most are the ones who ___.
items.audio:
Thank you all for coming this evening. My name is Rustam Karimov, and I have worked in computer security for fourteen years. Tonight I want to change the way you think about passwords, because most of the advice you have been given is, frankly, out of date. For years we were told to choose a short password full of strange symbols and to change it every ninety days. Today almost every expert, including me, thinks that was a mistake. When people are forced to change passwords all the time, they simply add a number at the end, so that Summer one becomes Summer two, and a thief can guess that in seconds.

What works much better is length. A password of sixteen characters made from four ordinary words, for example the name of a fruit, a street, a colour and a piece of furniture, is far harder to break than a short password with clever symbols. Notice that I said sixteen, not sixty. Nobody needs to type sixty characters, and the extra effort would not make you any safer. The words should be unrelated, though. A phrase from a famous song is not a good choice, because attackers try those first.

The second rule is never to use the same password twice. Last year a large shopping website lost the details of about eight million customers, and I mean eight, not eighty, although that was still a disaster. Within a day, criminals tried the same email addresses and passwords on banks and social networks. items.prompt: Where must visitors leave their phones?
items.answer: In the lockers by the entrance
items.audio:
Welcome to the Northfield Biology Laboratory. My name is Hannah, and I will be your guide for the next hour. Before we go in, I must go through a few rules. First, nobody may take photographs inside the building, so please leave your phones in the lockers by the entrance. Second, everybody has to wear safety goggles in the main laboratory. The only exception is for those of you who wear your own glasses, because the lenses are considered strong enough, but the goggles are still available if you prefer them. Third, please do not touch anything, however tempting it looks.

Our first stop is the freezer room. In here we keep thousands of samples at a temperature of minus eighty degrees. That is far colder than any kitchen freezer, so the door is heavy and the alarm sounds if it stays open for more than a minute. Last winter there was a power cut, and the emergency generator started at once, so we lost nothing. I should say that the freezers are the most expensive part of the building, and replacing one costs more than a family car.

Next we move to the microscope room, where about fifteen researchers work on cells from plants. Not fifty, as some visitors imagine, because the department is much smaller than people expect. I was told this morning that we would be visiting the robot room as well, but I have just learned that it is closed for repairs, so we will go to the seed bank instead. I am sorry about that, since the robots are usually the favourite part of the tour.

The seed bank is a quiet room where we store seeds from wild plants that are disappearing. Dr Bakhtiyor Aliev, who runs it, believes that these seeds may one day help farmers grow food in dry places. He often says that a seed is a tiny promise, and I rather like that idea. Each packet is labelled with the date, the place and the name of the collector. Some of the oldest packets are almost forty years old, and a few of them still grow perfectly well when tested.

Our last stop is the coffee room, which is the only place in the building where food and drink are allowed. Please do not carry your cup back into the corridor. If you have questions, I will be glad to answer them, and at the end I will give each of you a small packet of sunflower seeds as a souvenir. Shall we begin?
options: In the lockers by the entrance

items.prompt: Why did Jasur not become a footballer?
items.answer: His knees were not strong enough
items.audio:
Today in our series about people who build things, I am talking to Jasur Rakhimov, the chief engineer of the new river bridge in Samarkand. Jasur, congratulations on the opening. Thank you, but I should say that I will only relax when the first winter has passed. The interviewer asks how he became an engineer, and Jasur laughs. He says that as a boy he wanted to be a footballer, but his knees were not strong enough, and a teacher who noticed his talent for mathematics suggested a technical university instead. He now thinks it was the best advice anyone ever gave him.

The interviewer wants to know about the biggest problem on the project. Jasur says it was the decision about the material. At first the team planned to build the bridge out of steel, because it is lighter and quicker to assemble. However, in the second year the price of steel rose by almost a third, so they changed the plan and used reinforced concrete for the towers and steel only for the deck. He admits that he was not happy at the time, because he had spent months on the original design, but he now accepts that the new version is stronger and will need less maintenance.

The bridge is four hundred and eighty metres long and carries two lanes of traffic in each direction, as well as a wide path for walkers and cyclists. That path was Jasur's own idea. Some members of the committee thought it was a waste of space, but he argued that people in a city need to be able to cross a river without a car. In the end he won the argument, and he says that on a sunny Saturday the path is busier than the road.

The interviewer asks about the opening date. It was meant to be in May, but heavy rain in the spring flooded the work area and delayed the last stage by six weeks. Jasur says that nobody was angry about it, because safety matters more than a ceremony. He adds that two workers were slightly injured during the project, and he considers even that too many.

Asked about his future plans, Jasur says he would like a long holiday, preferably somewhere with no bridges. He then smiles and admits that he will probably spend it looking at the bridges anyway. His next job is a tunnel in the mountains, which, he says, will be far harder than anything he has done so far. The interviewer thanks him, and we will return after the music.
options: His knees were not strong enough

Today in our series about people who build things, I am talking to Jasur Rakhimov, the chief engineer of the new river bridge in Samarkand. Jasur, congratulations on the opening. Thank you, but I should say that I will only relax when the first winter has passed. The interviewer asks how he became an engineer, and Jasur laughs. He says that as a boy he wanted to be a footballer, but his knees were not strong enough, and a teacher who noticed his talent for mathematics suggested a technical university instead. He now thinks it was the best advice anyone ever gave him.

The interviewer wants to know about the biggest problem on the project. Jasur says it was the decision about the material. At first the team planned to build the bridge out of steel, because it is lighter and quicker to assemble. However, in the second year the price of steel rose by almost a third, so they changed the plan and used reinforced concrete for the towers and steel only for the deck. He admits that he was not happy at the time, because he had spent months on the original design, but he now accepts that the new version is stronger and will need less maintenance.

The bridge is four hundred and eighty metres long and carries two lanes of traffic in each direction, as well as a wide path for walkers and cyclists. That path was Jasur's own idea. Some members of the committee thought it was a waste of space, but he argued that people in a city need to be able to cross a river without a car. In the end he won the argument, and he says that on a sunny Saturday the path is busier than the road.

The interviewer asks about the opening date. It was meant to be in May, but heavy rain in the spring flooded the work area and delayed the last stage by six weeks. Jasur says that nobody was angry about it, because safety matters more than a ceremony. He adds that two workers were slightly injured during the project, and he considers even that too many.

Asked about his future plans, Jasur says he would like a long holiday, preferably somewhere with no bridges. He then smiles and admits that he will probably spend it looking at the bridges anyway. His next job is a tunnel in the mountains, which, he says, will be far harder than anything he has done so far. The interviewer thanks him, and we will return after the music.
items.explain: Steel is still used for the deck.

items.prompt: Which lift should visitors use today?
items.audio:
Welcome to the Riverside Museum of Science and Industry. This audio guide will lead you through four floors and take about ninety minutes, although you may stop it whenever you like. Please start on the ground floor, and note that the lift near the entrance is out of order today, so if you need a lift, use the one beside the café. The museum is open until half past five, and the last entry to the steam hall is a quarter to five, so I suggest that you visit the steam hall first.

In front of you stands the Hartley engine, which was built in eighteen sixty-three to pump water from a coal mine. It is one of the oldest working engines in the country, and, if you are lucky, you may see it in motion. A demonstration takes place at noon and again at two o'clock, not at one as some older leaflets say. The engine was the work of a young engineer called Thomas Hartley, who, rather surprisingly, never went to school. He taught himself to read from the labels on tool boxes, and his notebooks, which you can see in the glass case on your left, are full of careful drawings.

Please do not touch the machinery. The only object that you are allowed to touch on this floor is the red button beside the window, which makes a model of the engine move slowly so that you can understand how the pistons work. Children usually love it, but adults press it just as often.

Now take the stairs to the first floor, where the exhibition about electricity begins. Many visitors expect to see lamps and cables, but the star of this room is a huge glass sphere that makes real lightning. Every thirty minutes a guide switches it on, and you will hear a loud crack. If you are nervous about noise, you can wait in the corridor outside, which is quiet. People with heart problems are asked not to stand close to the sphere.

On the second floor you will find the space gallery, which many people consider the best part of the museum, though I personally prefer the clocks upstairs. The gallery contains a piece of rock from the moon, which we are allowed to display for only two months each year because of its value. This year it will be here until the end of November. Photographs are welcome everywhere, but please switch off the flash.

The shop on the ground floor sells books, models and postcards. If you show your ticket there, you will receive a discount of ten percent on anything except food. Thank you for visiting, and we hope you enjoy your day.
options: The one in the space gallery

items.prompt: How has Lena's attitude changed over the years?
items.audio:
Hello and welcome to Tomorrow Today. I am your host, Sevara, and this week we are asking whether artificial intelligence will soon replace doctors. My guest is Doctor Lena Fischer, who has spent nine years working on computer programs that read medical scans. Lena, many people are frightened by this subject. Are they right to be? Lena answers that she used to be quite optimistic, but over time she has become more careful. She explains that in her first years she believed that machines would do most of a doctor's work by the end of the decade. Now she thinks that was naive.

Sevara asks for an example. Lena describes a study in twelve hospitals, where a program looked at chest pictures and tried to find early signs of lung disease. In ninety out of a hundred cases, the program agreed with the senior doctors. That sounds impressive, but Lena points out that in the remaining cases it made mistakes that no human doctor would make, such as confusing a small piece of jewellery with a tumour. In other words, the program is very good on average, yet it can be strangely stupid in single cases.

Sevara wonders whether patients would accept advice from a machine. Lena says surveys show a surprising result: young people are more suspicious than older people. She had expected the opposite, but older patients, she thinks, simply care more about getting a fast answer. What nearly everyone agrees on is that a human being must give bad news, and that no program can replace a gentle voice in the room.

The conversation then turns to jobs. Sevara reads a message from a listener, a nurse called Gulbahor, who is worried that her hospital will cut staff to save money. Lena admits that this is a real danger, but she argues that the real problem is not the technology. It is the way managers decide to use it. In her own hospital, she says, the program saves each radiologist about one hour every day, and that hour is spent talking to patients rather than being removed from the budget. She adds that this is not the case everywhere, and she does not want to pretend that it is.

Towards the end, Sevara asks what Lena would tell a young person choosing a career. The answer is unexpected. She says she would still recommend medicine, because the doctors who learn to work with programs will be more valuable, not less. And what about her own plans? Lena says she is going to spend the next year testing the programs in two rural clinics, where there are few specialists. If they help there, she says, she will feel her work was worth it. Thank you, Lena, and thank you to everyone listening.
options: She has stopped working on scans

items.prompt: Why does Bobur want a new phone?
items.answer: His old one keeps switching off
items.audio:
Bobur walks into a phone shop on Saturday afternoon because his old phone, which he has had for four years, keeps switching itself off. A young assistant called Malika greets him and asks what he is looking for. items.prompt: What did Volta use between the metal discs?
items.audio:
Good morning, everyone. Today's lecture is about batteries, something you all use every day and almost nobody understands. Let us start with a little history. The first true battery was built by the Italian scientist Alessandro Volta around eighteen hundred. It was a pile of metal discs separated by cloth soaked in salty water, and it produced a small but steady electric current. For more than a century, batteries were heavy, weak and unreliable. The lithium-ion battery, which powers your phones, was first sold in nineteen ninety-one. Sorry, I wrote nineteen ninety-two on the slide, but that is wrong; the correct date is ninety-one, and I will correct it before I upload the notes.

How does it work? Inside the battery, lithium ions move from one side to the other when the battery is used, and move back again when it is charged. Think of it as a crowd of people moving from one room to another through a narrow door. When the crowd is in the full room, the battery is charged. The more times the crowd walks back and forth, the more the door wears out, and that is why every battery loses capacity eventually.

Now I want to destroy a few myths. First, many people believe it is bad to charge a phone overnight. In fact, modern phones stop charging when they are full, so this is not a serious problem. The real enemy is heat. A battery left in a hot car can lose much of its capacity in a single summer. Second, people say you should let a battery run completely flat before charging it. That was true of old nickel batteries, but for lithium-ion batteries it is the opposite. Keeping the charge between twenty and eighty percent makes the battery last roughly twice as long. I should be honest, though, and say that I do this myself only on my laptop, because with my phone I am too lazy.

What about the future? Many companies are developing solid-state batteries, which replace the liquid inside with a solid material. In theory they are safer and can store more energy. However, I have to be sceptical. Researchers have promised them for about fifteen years, and I will believe the promise when I can buy a car that uses one. Another approach is to use sodium, which is as common as salt and far cheaper than lithium, although a sodium battery is heavier for the same amount of energy.

Finally, recycling. At present, fewer than one battery in twenty is properly recycled in many countries. That is a waste of valuable metals, and I expect that governments will soon force producers to take back old batteries. For next week, please read the chapter on solar cells, and bring your questions.

Good morning, everyone. Today's lecture is about batteries, something you all use every day and almost nobody understands. Let us start with a little history. The first true battery was built by the Italian scientist Alessandro Volta around eighteen hundred. It was a pile of metal discs separated by cloth soaked in salty water, and it produced a small but steady electric current. For more than a century, batteries were heavy, weak and unreliable. The lithium-ion battery, which powers your phones, was first sold in nineteen ninety-one. Sorry, I wrote nineteen ninety-two on the slide, but that is wrong; the correct date is ninety-one, and I will correct it before I upload the notes.

How does it work? Inside the battery, lithium ions move from one side to the other when the battery is used, and move back again when it is charged. Think of it as a crowd of people moving from one room to another through a narrow door. When the crowd is in the full room, the battery is charged. The more times the crowd walks back and forth, the more the door wears out, and that is why every battery loses capacity eventually.

Now I want to destroy a few myths. First, many people believe it is bad to charge a phone overnight. In fact, modern phones stop charging when they are full, so this is not a serious problem. The real enemy is heat. A battery left in a hot car can lose much of its capacity in a single summer. Second, people say you should let a battery run completely flat before charging it. That was true of old nickel batteries, but for lithium-ion batteries it is the opposite. Keeping the charge between twenty and eighty percent makes the battery last roughly twice as long. I should be honest, though, and say that I do this myself only on my laptop, because with my phone I am too lazy.

What about the future? Many companies are developing solid-state batteries, which replace the liquid inside with a solid material. In theory they are safer and can store more energy. However, I have to be sceptical. Researchers have promised them for about fifteen years, and I will believe the promise when I can buy a car that uses one. Another approach is to use sodium, which is as common as salt and far cheaper than lithium, although a sodium battery is heavier for the same amount of energy.

Finally, recycling. At present, fewer than one battery in twenty is properly recycled in many countries. That is a waste of valuable metals, and I expect that governments will soon force producers to take back old batteries. For next week, please read the chapter on solar cells, and bring your questions.

items.prompt: Who is Kamila?
items.answer: One of the founders of the company
items.audio:
Good afternoon, everybody, and thank you for joining our online launch event. I am Kamila Yusupova, one of the founders of Busly, a small company from Tashkent that has spent two years building an application for people who travel by city bus. I want to tell you what the app does, why we made it, and what changes we have made since the first plan.

The idea came from a very ordinary frustration. My co-founder, Daniel, and I used to wait for the same bus every morning, never knowing whether it was three minutes or thirty minutes away. Official timetables were of little use, because buses are often late. So we asked drivers to install a small tracker, and now the app shows every bus on a map in real time. You simply choose your stop, and it tells you how many minutes remain. In tests, the forecast was correct within one minute in nine cases out of ten.

Originally we planned to launch in May. However, the testing showed that the app drained the battery too quickly, so we spent six extra weeks rewriting the code, and the launch moved to the middle of June. We think it was worth the wait. Today the app uses about half as much power as the first version. Another change concerns the system. We had intended to release the app for Android and for iPhone on the same day, but the approval process for iPhones is slower than we expected. So the Android version is available from today, and the iPhone version should follow in about a month. We apologise to those of you with iPhones. There is no version for tablets yet, and we have no date for it.

Now the question that everybody asks: how much does it cost? For the first three months, everything is free. After that, the basic service, which includes the map and the forecasts, will remain free forever. A subscription of three dollars a month adds extra features such as alerts when your bus is late and a plan that suggests the fastest route, including changes between lines. We debated for a long time whether to charge at all, and some people on the team wanted the whole app to be free. In the end we decided that a small income would let us keep improving it without advertisements.

Finally, we want to thank the drivers, who agreed to use the trackers without receiving any money, and the students at the technical university who helped us during the tests. The first fifty people to download the app today will receive a free six-month subscription. Please share it with your friends, and let us know what you think.
options: One of the founders of the company

items.prompt: How long will the trial continue?
items.audio:
In tonight's regional news, residents of the village of Llanfair in Wales have spent the last six months watching small drones carry medicine across the hills, and today the company running the trial announced that it will continue for another year. The experiment began last spring, when a local pharmacy, which is almost twenty kilometres from the nearest hospital, started using drones to deliver urgent prescriptions to farms that are hard to reach by road.

The pharmacist, Owen Parry, told our reporter that the service has changed his work. Before the trial, he often had to drive over narrow mountain roads for up to forty minutes to deliver a single package of tablets. Now a drone makes the same journey in eight minutes. Not eighteen, he joked, although in bad weather it can take that long. The drones can carry up to two kilograms, which is enough for most medicines but too little for large oxygen bottles, so those still arrive by van.

The company says that in the first six months the drones flew about nine hundred deliveries, and only twelve of them failed, mostly because of strong wind. In those cases the packages were returned to the pharmacy and delivered by car instead. The company is proud of the record, though it admits that it has not yet tested the drones in snow. That will be the real challenge during the coming winter.

Not everybody is delighted. Several residents complain that the drones are noisy, especially in the early morning, and one woman said that her horses have become nervous. The company has promised to change the flight paths so that the machines avoid the areas where most of the complaints came from, and it will also stop flights before seven in the morning. A local councillor, Eleri Davies, said that she supports the trial in principle but wants to be sure that the benefits are not outweighed by the disturbance. She added that she had personally counted fourteen flights over her house in a single afternoon, which she thought was too many.

Despite the complaints, a survey carried out last month suggests that most villagers are in favour. About seventy percent said they want the service to continue, while fifteen percent were against and the rest did not mind. One elderly farmer, who depends on regular medicine, said the drones had given him a feeling of security that he had not had for years. The company now hopes to expand the service to two other valleys, if it receives permission from the aviation authority later this year. That is all from Llanfair. Back to the studio.

items.prompt: How long has Mrs Okafor worked at the dealership?
items.audio:
Good evening, and thank you for braving the rain. My name is Mrs Okafor, and I have worked at this dealership for eleven years. Tonight I will talk about what it is really like to own an electric car, because many of you came with questions, and I have noticed that the same worries come up every time. I will try to be honest, even when that means telling you things the brochures leave out.

The first worry is range. The car we are looking at tonight can travel about three hundred and twenty kilometres on a full charge, according to the official test. In real life, you should expect somewhat less. In winter, when you use the heater and the battery is cold, the range can fall by about a fifth, so you might get only about two hundred and fifty. I always tell customers to plan with the smaller number. That said, the average driver here travels about forty kilometres a day, so most people never get anywhere near the limit.

The second worry is charging. If you have a garage or a private parking space, you can install a charger at home, which costs around eight hundred pounds including fitting, and the car will be full by the morning. Sorry, I should correct myself: eight hundred is the price of the charger alone, and fitting is extra, between one and two hundred pounds depending on your wiring. Anyone who lives in a block of flats will find life harder, since you need permission from the owner of the building. In that case you will rely on public chargers, and I would think carefully before buying.

The third worry is cost. An electric car is more expensive to buy, though cheaper to run. A full charge at home costs about as much as a cup of coffee in the city centre, while the same distance in a petrol car would cost five times as much. Maintenance is also lower, because there is no oil to change and fewer moving parts. However, the battery will eventually lose capacity, and replacing it after many years can be very costly. Most manufacturers offer a guarantee of eight years, which I consider fair.

Some of you have asked whether I drive an electric car myself. I do, but I did not at first. I was against the idea for years, because I thought the cars were slow and strange, and I only changed my mind when my son borrowed one for a weekend and brought it back full of enthusiasm. Now I would never go back. Please enjoy the refreshments at the back, and I will answer your questions one by one.

items.prompt: How many projects are there this year?
items.audio:
It is Thursday, the day of the school science fair, and Ms Ibragimova, the physics teacher who organised it, is speaking to the judges before the doors open. Thank you all for coming, she says. This year we have forty-two projects, which is a record, and I am afraid the weather has caused us a small problem. We planned to show the solar projects in the yard, but the forecast is for rain all afternoon, so everything will be indoors in the sports hall. The judges will therefore start at ten, not at nine as it says on your timetable, because the caretaker needs an extra hour to arrange the tables.

She then describes the projects the judges should look for. The first is by a boy named Temur, who built a solar oven out of a pizza box and aluminium foil. He claims that it can bake a biscuit in forty minutes on a sunny day, although his experiment last week gave a result of fifty minutes, so please ask him about the difference. The second is by two girls, Aisha and Nora, who tested whether plants grow faster when they listen to music. Ms Ibragimova admits that she was sceptical at first, because the idea sounds more like a joke than a science project. However, the girls kept careful records for six weeks, and she was impressed. Their result was that the plants with classical music grew slightly taller, but the difference was so small that it could be an accident, and, to their credit, they say so in their report.

The third project is a water filter made by Jamshid from sand, stones and charcoal. It cleans muddy water well enough to see through, but he does not claim that it is safe to drink, and the judges should not drink it either. Ms Ibragimova adds that, of all the projects, this one is probably the most useful in practice, and she would like the judges to look at it carefully.

Next, the rules for judging. Each judge gives marks out of ten for three things: the idea, the quality of the experiment, and the explanation. Marks for how the project looks should not count, since a plain board with a good experiment is better than a colourful one without. The winner will receive a prize of one hundred pounds for the school's science club, and second and third places will receive books. The results will be announced at half past three in the main hall, and parents are invited.

Finally, she thanks everyone and says that she hopes the judges will be kind, because some of the students have not slept for two nights. The doors open at ten, and the first group of visitors is already waiting outside in the rain.

items.prompt: How many people are at the workshop?
items.audio:
Welcome, everyone, to the Saturday workshop at the Greenway Makerspace. My name is Arman, and I will be teaching you the basics of three-dimensional printing today. There are nine of you, which is a good number, because we have only four printers and you will have to share. I know that some of you were hoping to print a complete model of a car, but I have to be realistic. The biggest object that our printers can make is about as large as a loaf of bread, and a small object can still take several hours, so today we will print something simple.

Let me start with how a printer works. It melts a thin plastic thread, which we call filament, and lays it down in very thin layers, one on top of another, until the object is finished. The plastic we use today is made from corn and is not harmful, although it does have a slightly sweet smell. The nozzle, where the plastic comes out, reaches two hundred degrees, so nobody may touch it, not even to check whether it is hot. Please remember that, because every year somebody forgets.

To make an object, you first need a design. You can draw one on the computer, which is what we will do this morning, or you can download one from a website. I usually recommend downloading first, because drawing is harder than it looks, and a bad first experience is discouraging. However, we will spend an hour on drawing anyway, because I think you will understand the printing better afterwards. After that, the program cuts your design into layers and sends it to the printer. The little key ring that you are going to make takes about forty minutes. Not fourteen, as one lady asked, but forty, so please be patient.

Things often go wrong, and I want you to know that this is completely normal. The most common problem is that the first layer does not stick to the plate, so the whole object moves and turns into a tangle of plastic. We call this spaghetti, for obvious reasons. If it happens to you, do not be embarrassed. Stop the printer, clean the plate, and start again. I have been printing for six years, and I still produce spaghetti about once a week.

The workshop costs thirty-five pounds, which includes the plastic for your key ring. Anyone who wants to carry on afterwards can buy a monthly membership for twenty pounds, which gives you access to the printers every evening except Sunday. We have changed this recently, because the printers used to be open on Sundays as well, but too few people came. Right, shall we turn on the computers and begin?

I know that some of you were hoping to print a complete model of a car, but I have to be realistic. The biggest object that our printers can make is about as large as a loaf of bread, and a small object can still take several hours, so today we will print something simple.

Let me start with how a printer works. It melts a thin plastic thread, which we call filament, and lays it down in very thin layers, one on top of another, until the object is finished. The plastic we use today is made from corn and is not harmful, although it does have a slightly sweet smell. The nozzle, where the plastic comes out, reaches two hundred degrees, so nobody may touch it, not even to check whether it is hot. Please remember that, because every year somebody forgets.

To make an object, you first need a design. You can draw one on the computer, which is what we will do this morning, or you can download one from a website. I usually recommend downloading first, because drawing is harder than it looks, and a bad first experience is discouraging. However, we will spend an hour on drawing anyway, because I think you will understand the printing better afterwards. After that, the program cuts your design into layers and sends it to the printer. The little key ring that you are going to make takes about forty minutes. Not fourteen, as one lady asked, but forty, so please be patient.

Things often go wrong, and I want you to know that this is completely normal. The most common problem is that the first layer does not stick to the plate, so the whole object moves and turns into a tangle of plastic. We call this spaghetti, for obvious reasons. If it happens to you, do not be embarrassed. Stop the printer, clean the plate, and start again. I have been printing for six years, and I still produce spaghetti about once a week.

The workshop costs thirty-five pounds, which includes the plastic for your key ring. Anyone who wants to carry on afterwards can buy a monthly membership for twenty pounds, which gives you access to the printers every evening except Sunday. We have changed this recently, because the printers used to be open on Sundays as well, but too few people came. Right, shall we turn on the computers and begin?

items.prompt: Why does Peter refuse the tea?
items.audio:
On Tuesday morning a technician called Peter arrives at the flat of a woman named Zilola, who has ordered a smart home package. She greets him at the door and offers him tea, which he politely refuses because he has another appointment in two hours. Peter looks around and asks what she hopes to achieve. Zilola explains that she travels a lot for work and wants to control the heating from her phone, so that the flat is warm when she returns and not wasting energy while she is away. She also says that she originally wanted four cameras, one in each room.

Peter stops her there. He says that he has installed many systems and that cameras inside a home are, in his opinion, rarely a good idea. A hacked camera would show a stranger the inside of her flat, and the more devices she connects, the more doors she opens for criminals. He suggests door and window sensors instead, which cost much less and tell her when something is opened, without recording any pictures. After some thought, Zilola agrees to change her plan. She will have one camera at the front door only, and sensors on the windows.

Next they discuss the thermostat. Peter shows her a small white device and explains that it learns when she is usually at home. After about a week, it will switch the heating on and off by itself. Zilola is doubtful, as her old thermostat was simple and she liked that. Peter admits that the new one is more complicated, but he says it can save about fifteen percent on her bills, not fifty as the advertisement claims. He is careful to correct the number, because he does not want her to be disappointed. She decides to give it a try, with the right to return it within thirty days.

Then comes the wireless connection. Peter tests the signal in each room and finds that it is weak in the bedroom, which is at the far end of the flat. He recommends a small extender, which costs twenty-five pounds and is not included in the package. Zilola is a little annoyed, as she had thought that everything was included. Peter shows her the order form, where the extender is listed as optional, and she accepts that she misread it. She buys it.

The work takes about three hours, rather than two, because one sensor refuses to connect. Peter finally solves the problem by moving it a few centimetres. Before he leaves, he teaches her to use the application and gives her a card with the number to call if something goes wrong. He says that the first week is usually the hardest, and that the system will soon feel as natural as using a light switch. Zilola thanks him and says that she is looking forward to tonight, when she will test it from the sofa.

items.prompt: How many families have accepted a place in the shelter?
items.audio:
Good evening, and welcome to the nine o'clock news on Radio Calder Valley. Our main story tonight is the flooding in the town of Marwick, where the river burst its banks early this morning. Police say that about three hundred and fifty residents were asked to leave their homes, although only thirteen families have so far accepted a place in the emergency shelter at the sports hall. Most people have chosen to stay with relatives instead. A council spokeswoman, Helen Draper, first told reporters that the water had reached two metres in the high street, but an hour later she corrected herself and said it was one and a half metres, which is still the highest level since nineteen ninety-eight.

The main road bridge has been closed to all traffic, and engineers will inspect it tomorrow morning. Buses will not run between Marwick and Thornby until at least Friday, but the railway line is open, and the company has promised extra trains at seven and again at eight in the morning. Drivers are told not to use the old mill road, which many people suggested as a shortcut, because it is also under water. Schools in the town will stay shut tomorrow, though the primary school in the neighbouring village of Ashby will open as normal.

Our reporter, Dilnoza Rakhimova, spoke to a baker whose shop was flooded. Mr Okafor said he had not expected the river to rise so quickly, because the last warning, on Sunday, had said the rain would stop by midnight. He admitted that he had ignored a text message from the council the previous evening, thinking it was an advertisement. He lost all his flour and two ovens, but he says he is not angry with anyone. What bothers him, he said, is that the flood barrier promised after the last flood was never built. The council answered that the money had been approved but that building work was delayed by a dispute over the land, and that it would now start in spring.

Volunteers have been brilliant, according to the shelter manager. More than sixty people turned up with blankets and hot food, so the organisers have asked people to stop bringing clothes, since the hall is already full of them. What is still needed is bottled water and baby food, and these can be left at the library until noon. items.prompt: How long does Brenda's journey take now?
items.audio:
Welcome back to Morning Talk, I'm Jamshid Karimov, and today we are discussing the new bus lane on Victoria Street, which opened on Monday. Our first caller was Brenda, a nurse, who said she was delighted. Her journey to the hospital used to take fifty minutes, and now it takes thirty-five. Jamshid reminded her that the council had promised twenty-five, and Brenda laughed and said she would happily accept any improvement at all, because she starts work at six and hates being late.

The second caller, a taxi driver named Gareth, was far less happy. He said the bus lane was a ridiculous idea because taxis are not allowed to use it, and he had already lost two customers who refused to wait in traffic. He admitted, however, that he had not read the whole leaflet, and Jamshid explained that taxis may use the lane after seven in the evening. Gareth said that was fine for night work but useless for him, since most of his regular passengers travel in the morning. He suggested that the council should have asked drivers before spending the money, and he was surprised to hear that a public meeting had taken place in March.

Next came a shopkeeper, Mrs Yusupova, who owns a flower stall near the market. She was not against the lane itself, but she complained that delivery vans could no longer stop outside her shop. Her supplier now has to park two streets away and carry the boxes, which takes an extra twenty minutes. She said that she had called the council twice, and nobody had answered. Jamshid promised to pass her number to the transport department, which he said would be listening to the programme. At that moment a producer told him that the department's director, Mr Lindqvist, was already on the other line.

Mr Lindqvist said he understood the complaints and would allow vans to stop in the lane for ten minutes between ten and noon, starting from next month. He did not agree, though, that the scheme should be cancelled. Fines for private cars in the lane, he said, would begin only after a fortnight of warnings, so nobody has been charged yet. The last caller, a student called Marcus, said that he would prefer a cycle path to a bus lane, and that he had stopped cycling to college because of the fumes. Jamshid thanked everybody and said the council would publish traffic figures in six weeks. After the news and weather, we turn to the story of a dog that has learned to catch the bus on its own.

items.prompt: Why was the ceremony held indoors?
items.audio:
Good afternoon, everybody, and thank you for coming in spite of the rain. I had planned to cut the ribbon outside, but as you can see, we have moved everything into the reading hall, which, I must say, looks better than I imagined. I am Mayor Aziza Nurmatova, and it gives me great pleasure to reopen the Central Library after eighteen months of building work. When we started, I promised it would take twelve months. I was wrong, and I apologise, but I hope you will agree that the delay was worth it.

Let me remind you why we did this. Fifteen years ago the building had no lift, and an elderly visitor had to be carried up the stairs. Today there are two lifts, a ramp, and a quiet room for people who find crowds difficult. The collection has grown to nearly ninety thousand books, though I should point out that only about half are on the open shelves; the rest are in the basement and can be ordered at the desk. Some critics said we should have spent the money on schools instead. I understand that view, and I do not think it is silly. But the library is where many children do their homework when it is too noisy at home.

The total cost was four point two million, which is more than the three point eight million in the original budget. Most of the difference came from the roof, which turned out to be in a much worse state than the surveyors had said. Two thirds of the money came from the national lottery fund, and the remainder from the city, so I want to thank every person in this country who bought a lottery ticket. I also want to thank Mr Haddad, the chief architect, who, I am told, has not had a proper holiday since the summer before last.

Now a few practical things. The library will open at eight in the morning and close at nine at night, except on Sundays, when it closes at five. Membership is free for anyone under eighteen, and for adults it costs five pounds a year, though pensioners pay nothing. There will be no fines for late books during the first month, which I expect will make some of you very happy. Finally, a change to the programme: the author who was supposed to give today's talk is ill, so instead our youngest member, nine-year-old Timur, will read from his favourite story. I am told that he has been practising for a week and is not at all nervous. Please welcome him, and enjoy your library.

items.prompt: Why did Daniel first start volunteering?
items.audio:
In today's programme, our reporter Kamila Ergasheva interviews Daniel Mbeki, a volunteer at the Eastside Food Bank. Daniel explains that he began helping three years ago, soon after he lost his job as a warehouse manager. He expected to stay for a month, until he found something new, but he now works there four days a week, even though he has been employed again since last spring. Kamila asks whether that annoys his new employer, and Daniel laughs and says that his boss actually lets him leave early on Thursdays.

Kamila asks what surprises people most. Daniel answers that visitors are rarely who you expect. Many are not unemployed at all. They are teachers, drivers or care workers whose wages simply do not cover rent and food in the same month. Last winter the food bank served about four hundred families a week, compared with two hundred and forty the winter before. He says he used to believe that the problem would shrink as the economy recovered, but he no longer thinks so, because prices have risen faster than salaries.

Asked about the biggest difficulty, Daniel does not mention money. It is storage. Fresh vegetables arrive on Mondays and Fridays, and half of them must be handed out within two days. The charity has one small cold room, which holds only a third of what is delivered. A supermarket has offered a second fridge, but the volunteers cannot accept it until they find an electrician who will install it without charge. Daniel jokes that if any listener knows one, he will make that person a cup of tea every day for a year. Kamila points out that he does not drink tea himself, only coffee, and Daniel says that is exactly why the offer is generous.

She then asks whether he has ever wanted to give up. He says only once, last December, when a man shouted at him because the bread had run out. Afterwards he sat in the car for ten minutes feeling miserable. But the next morning the same man came back to apologise and stayed to help carry boxes, and he is still there. Daniel believes the lesson is not to take anger personally. He adds that the food bank always needs drivers more than cash, because the van is old and fuel is expensive. People who are interested can call the number on the website, or simply come on a Saturday morning, when new volunteers are given a short training session before they start. Daniel says there is no need to be strong; patience matters much more than muscles.

items.prompt: How long did it take Josiah Pell to save for his press?
items.audio:
In the early eighteen hundreds, the market town of Eldermere had no newspaper at all. News arrived by letter, by coach, or, most often, by gossip. That changed in eighteen twenty-three, when a young printer named Josiah Pell bought a second-hand press for forty pounds, a sum which took him six years to save. Many people assumed that he would fail within a year. In fact the first issue, which appeared on a rainy Saturday in October, sold out by noon, although it contained only four pages and two of them were advertisements.

Pell was not a talented writer, and he knew it. Instead he relied on a network of correspondents: a vicar who sent reports from the villages, a coach driver who collected stories along his route, and, rather surprisingly, a schoolgirl called Martha Lowe, who wrote about local events under a man's name because her father disapproved. Historians once believed that the paper's best articles were by Pell himself. It was only in nineteen sixty, when a box of letters was discovered in an attic, that the truth emerged, and Martha is now remembered as the town's first woman journalist.

The paper was never without trouble. In eighteen thirty-one the town's magistrate sued Pell for printing a story that said he had taken bribes. Pell lost the case and paid a heavy fine, but the publicity doubled his readers. Thereafter he was more careful, checking each claim with two sources, a habit which he called his golden rule. Ironically, the one big mistake of his career was not about corruption at all. In eighteen forty he announced the death of a popular doctor, who walked into the printing office the next day, very much alive, and asked for a copy to keep.

By the eighteen sixties the paper had sixteen pages, a staff of nine and a circulation of three thousand, which was remarkable for a town of only eleven thousand people. Then came the telegraph and the railway, and national newspapers began to arrive by the morning train. Local readers did not abandon Pell's paper, but they began to treat it differently: no longer as the place where they learned what had happened in the world, but as the place where they learned what had happened in their street. Some experts argue that this is exactly the role local media should play today. The press itself was eventually sold for scrap, but the doctor's copy of that famous issue is still on display in the town museum.

items.prompt: Why did the meeting start late?
items.answer: The chairperson had to find more chairs
items.audio:
The meeting at Greenfield Community Centre began ten minutes late, because the chairperson, Mrs Odinaeva, had to find enough chairs. About ninety residents had come, far more than the thirty the organisers expected, which she took as proof that people care about the old playground on Mill Lane. She began by explaining the situation: the council had offered to pay half the cost of a new playground, provided the neighbourhood could raise the other half, which comes to about eighteen thousand.

The first speaker, a father named Rob, argued that safety was the only issue that mattered. Two children had broken arms last year on the old climbing frame, and he thought it should be removed immediately. A retired teacher, Mr Samadov, disagreed. He said that children needed some risk, and that the real problem was the broken fence, which let dogs in. Several people clapped, though a young mother pointed out that she would rather have a fence and a safe climbing frame. Mrs Odinaeva suggested that it was not necessary to choose between the two.

Then came the question of money. A local café owner, Fatima, offered to hold a cake sale every Sunday for three months, and a builder promised to lend a digger free of charge for two days. Someone suggested asking the big supermarket on the ring road, but Mr Samadov warned that it had refused a similar request last year. Another man proposed that every household should pay twenty a year, and this idea was received badly. One woman said that many pensioners could not afford it, and that a voluntary contribution would be fairer. After a lot of discussion the chairperson put the idea aside.

The most surprising moment came near the end. A twelve-year-old boy, Anvar, stood up at the back and asked whether anyone had asked the children what they wanted. There was a short silence, and then Mrs Odinaeva admitted that nobody had. She promised to invite pupils from the local school to draw their ideas, and she said the final design would not be chosen until all the drawings had been seen. The vote was therefore postponed from next Tuesday to the end of the month. Before everyone left, volunteers signed up for a working group of seven, which will meet at the café on Thursday evenings. Mrs Odinaeva closed the meeting at nine, apologising for the length, but several people told her afterwards it was the most interesting meeting they had ever attended.

About ninety residents had come, far more than the thirty the organisers expected, which she took as proof that people care about the old playground on Mill Lane. She began by explaining the situation: the council had offered to pay half the cost of a new playground, provided the neighbourhood could raise the other half, which comes to about eighteen thousand.

The first speaker, a father named Rob, argued that safety was the only issue that mattered. Two children had broken arms last year on the old climbing frame, and he thought it should be removed immediately. A retired teacher, Mr Samadov, disagreed. He said that children needed some risk, and that the real problem was the broken fence, which let dogs in. Several people clapped, though a young mother pointed out that she would rather have a fence and a safe climbing frame. Mrs Odinaeva suggested that it was not necessary to choose between the two.

Then came the question of money. A local café owner, Fatima, offered to hold a cake sale every Sunday for three months, and a builder promised to lend a digger free of charge for two days. Someone suggested asking the big supermarket on the ring road, but Mr Samadov warned that it had refused a similar request last year. Another man proposed that every household should pay twenty a year, and this idea was received badly. One woman said that many pensioners could not afford it, and that a voluntary contribution would be fairer. After a lot of discussion the chairperson put the idea aside.

The most surprising moment came near the end. A twelve-year-old boy, Anvar, stood up at the back and asked whether anyone had asked the children what they wanted. There was a short silence, and then Mrs Odinaeva admitted that nobody had. She promised to invite pupils from the local school to draw their ideas, and she said the final design would not be chosen until all the drawings had been seen. The vote was therefore postponed from next Tuesday to the end of the month. Before everyone left, volunteers signed up for a working group of seven, which will meet at the café on Thursday evenings. Mrs Odinaeva closed the meeting at nine, apologising for the length, but several people told her afterwards it was the most interesting meeting they had ever attended.

items.prompt: When is the interview with the port director?
items.audio:
Hi Sanjar, it's Leila. I'm calling from the train, so forgive me if the line breaks up. I wanted to update you on the harbour story before tomorrow's meeting. First, the good news: the interview with the port director is confirmed. I said Wednesday in my email, but it's actually Thursday at half past two, because he has a hospital appointment on Wednesday. Please tell Marta, because she's booked the photographer for the wrong day.

Second, the numbers. I told you last week that the port had lost about fifteen jobs. I've now seen the official document, and the figure is fifty, not fifteen. I'm sorry about the mistake; I misread the page. It's still a story, and, frankly, a bigger one. The company says that the jobs were lost through natural leaving and retirement, but two former workers I spoke to yesterday claim that at least twenty of them were told to go. Neither wants their name used, so we must be careful. I'd like to use the phrase according to former employees, not sources close to the port, which sounds too vague.

Third, the problem. The union leader, Mr Castellano, who promised to talk to me, has gone quiet. His assistant says he is travelling until Monday, but I saw him in the café opposite the station this morning. I don't think he is lying exactly; I think he's nervous because of the legal letter the company sent him. So I won't push him this week. If we publish on Saturday, we can say he declined to comment, but I'd prefer to wait until we have his side, even if that means missing the weekend edition. I know you'll say we can't afford to wait, because the rival paper is chasing the same story. My feeling is that they only have the first set of figures, the wrong ones, and will probably repeat them.

Last thing. Don't worry about the photographs of the empty offices; I took them myself on my phone and they're perfectly good, though not for the front page. Could you ask the legal department whether they can look at my draft by Friday morning? I'll send it at lunchtime. Oh, and the train's just arriving, so I need to go. I'm back in the office on Tuesday, but on Monday I'll be working from home, so call me there if you need anything. And please, no more jokes about my handwriting at the meeting. Right, speak soon. Bye.

items.prompt: Why was the elderly woman wearing her coat indoors?
items.audio:
Good evening. My name is Dr Rustam Aliev, and I am speaking to you on behalf of Warm Homes, a small charity which helps elderly people in our region heat their homes through the winter. Last January, a volunteer visited a woman of eighty-four who was wearing her coat indoors because she could not afford to turn on the heating. She told us she was fine and did not want to be a bother. That is what we hear again and again, and it is the reason I am asking for your help tonight.

Let me give you some figures. Last winter we helped one thousand two hundred households, and this year the number of requests is already thirteen hundred, although the real winter has not even started. At the same time, our government grant has been cut by a fifth. Please do not misunderstand me, I am not blaming anybody; the officials were honest and explained that they had to make difficult choices. But the result is a gap of ninety thousand, and we have until the end of November to close it.

What will your money do? A gift of twenty will pay for a week of heating for one household. Forty will buy proper insulation for a window, which can reduce bills by ten percent for years. One hundred will pay for a full check of a home by a trained adviser, who also helps with applications for benefits that many older people do not realise they can claim. You might think that we should simply give money, but our experience shows that practical help works better. Some people even refuse cash, because they feel ashamed, but they happily accept a free visit from a neighbour who brings a draught excluder.

There are three ways to help. You can donate through our website, or by ringing the number I will give you in a moment. You can volunteer: we need drivers and people who can spare two hours on a Saturday. Or you can simply knock on the door of an older neighbour tonight and ask if they are warm enough. This costs nothing at all, and it may be the most valuable thing of the three. Finally, a small announcement: a local firm has promised to match every donation made this week, so your twenty becomes forty. The number is oh eight hundred, five five five, one one two. Thank you for listening, and please keep your neighbours warm.

items.prompt: Why is Walter against Sunday opening?
items.answer: He missed family lunches when he worked Sundays
items.audio:
For this week's programme, our reporter Nargiza spent a morning in the main square asking passers-by whether shops in the city should be allowed to open on Sundays. She said the first person she stopped, a retired bus driver named Walter, was firmly against the idea. He worked on Sundays for thirty years and missed almost every family lunch. He said nobody should have to do that, and certainly not for the sake of a few extra sales.

The second person, a student called Ines, took the opposite view. She works in a bookshop during the week and studies in the evenings, so Sunday is the only day she can shop. She said that closing shops on the one day people are free is simply illogical. But when Nargiza asked whether she would be happy to work on Sundays herself, Ines hesitated and then said she would, as long as she was paid double. Nargiza noticed that most younger people gave a similar answer: they were in favour, but only with better pay.

A woman with two small children, Mrs Tashkentova, said she was undecided. Sunday opening would be convenient, but she worried about the smaller shops. Big supermarkets can afford extra staff, whereas the family bakery next to her house cannot, so customers would drift away from it. A man selling newspapers from a kiosk said he did not care in the least, because he has opened every day of the year since the nineteen nineties, including Christmas, and nobody has ever thanked him for it. Nargiza says he said this with a smile.

Out of fifty people questioned, twenty-two supported Sunday opening, eighteen were against, and ten could not decide. Nargiza pointed out that this is hardly scientific, as the survey took place in a square near several cafés and so probably reached more young people than elderly ones. The mayor's office has said it will not make a decision until the autumn, when a proper study is finished. Meanwhile one shop owner, who asked not to be named, told Nargiza privately that he is already preparing, and has hired two extra assistants, just in case. Her conclusion was that almost everybody agreed on one point: if shops do open, the workers must be treated fairly. Next week she will ask people about the price of coffee.
options: He missed family lunches when he worked Sundays
