items.prompt: Who did Oksana mostly find at the market?
items.audio:
Welcome to Street Level, the podcast about how we really live in our cities. I'm your host, Oksana, and this week I'm in the old harbour district, where a night market has appeared on Friday evenings over the past two years. When I arrived at seven, I assumed I would find tourists. In fact, I found mostly local people, many of them carrying their own shopping bags, and a queue for dumplings that was easily thirty metres long.

I spoke first to Kofi, who runs a stall selling grilled corn. He told me that he used to work in an office and left his job two years ago, a decision that his mother still calls crazy. He now earns less money, he admits, but he is much happier, and he says the market has given him something unexpected: friends. The man at the next stall lends him a gas bottle when his own runs out, and in return Kofi supplies him with lunch. Then he stopped himself and said that, strictly speaking, he gives him dinner, because the market opens in the evening.

Not everyone is delighted. A woman who lives above the square, Mrs Bianchi, told me the noise continues until midnight and the street smells of frying oil on Saturday mornings. She does not wish to close the market, she said, only to make it end one hour earlier. The organiser, Tomas, replied that he had already agreed to stop music at ten, and that the cleaning team starts at eleven, so by dawn there is nothing left. They disagree about whether that is true. Frankly, when I walked through the square at eight on Saturday morning, it was clean, though there was a slight smell of onions.

Why does this matter for the city? Urban planners I talked to say that evening markets bring life to streets that are empty after five. Shops nearby report that their sales on Friday have risen by about a quarter, though a restaurant owner complained that the market takes away his customers. I think both things are true. There are, however, plans to move the market to a car park outside the centre, because of the rent the harbour authority wants. Tomas says that would destroy it, since people come precisely because it is where they can walk after work. I'm inclined to agree. Next week we visit a rooftop garden. Until then, walk somewhere new.

items.prompt: What did the research on students show?
items.answer: Most could not tell an article from an advert
items.audio:
Thank you all for coming to this workshop on spotting false stories online. My name is Professor Imani Okoro, and I teach media studies at the university. I'd like to begin with an uncomfortable fact: when researchers tested students last year, about three quarters could not tell a real news article from a paid advertisement that looked like one. I assumed that older people would be worse, but they were actually slightly better, perhaps because they still read printed papers.

Let me describe a simple method called lateral reading. Most people, when they see a strange website, stay on that website and read it carefully. Professional fact-checkers do the opposite: they leave the page after a few seconds and search for what other sources say about it. This takes about two minutes, not twenty, and it works much better. Please don't think that you must become a detective. You only need to ask three questions. Who is behind this? What is the evidence? And what do other sources say?

Here is a true example. Last spring a photograph went around showing a flooded airport, with people swimming in the terminal. It was shared more than two hundred thousand times. A journalist in my class needed only five minutes to discover that the picture came from a film trailer, made two years earlier. What interests me is that many of those who shared it did not believe it was real. They simply thought it was funny, or they wanted to show that they were worried about climate change. Intentions matter, but the effect is the same: a false picture becomes part of what people remember.

Now a word about our own habits. Most of us share a story because of how it makes us feel, not because we believe it. So here is my rule: if a headline makes you very angry, wait ten minutes before you share it. It sounds simple, and it is not a perfect solution, but studies suggest that it reduces sharing of false material by almost a third. I would add one warning, though. Do not become so suspicious that you believe nothing. That is just as dangerous, because then even honest reporters cannot persuade you of anything. After the break, you will work in pairs on three examples I have prepared. Please bring your phones, and not just your laptops, because most false stories travel on phones. The session ends at four, not at five, as the programme says, since the room is needed afterwards.
options: Most could not tell an article from an advert

items.prompt: What went wrong at the start of the debate?
items.audio:
Last night's debate between the two candidates for mayor of Hartley took place in the town hall, in front of about four hundred people. The incumbent, Councillor Patricia Moyo, and her challenger, the local doctor Farhod Ismoilov, had agreed on three subjects: housing, transport and the future of the old swimming pool. The evening started badly when the microphone for Dr Ismoilov failed and he had to speak without it for the first ten minutes, which he said afterwards was good practice for a doctor who has often had to shout across a crowded waiting room.

On housing, both candidates agreed that the town needs more homes, but they disagreed about where to build them. Councillor Moyo wants new flats on the former factory site by the canal, which would provide about two hundred homes. Dr Ismoilov thinks that is too crowded, and prefers smaller developments on the edge of town, near the school. When asked about the green fields there, he said he would protect the best of them, but not all, and some in the audience booed. He answered that honesty was better than a promise he could not keep.

The most heated exchange was about transport. Councillor Moyo defended the increase in parking charges, saying it paid for new buses. Dr Ismoilov replied that the buses were still not reliable and that parking prices had driven away customers from the market. She answered that the number of bus passengers had gone up by twelve percent, and he accused her of choosing figures that suited her. At that point the host, a retired teacher, reminded them politely that the audience had not come to listen to an argument, but to learn what each candidate would do. Both apologised and, to general surprise, shook hands.

The swimming pool, which closed last year, produced the biggest surprise. Everyone expected the candidates to promise to reopen it. Instead, Councillor Moyo said she would not, because it would cost one million a year to run and the town simply could not pay. Dr Ismoilov said he would reopen it, but only if the neighbouring towns shared the costs. Most commentators think he gained more support from this answer, although an opinion poll published this morning shows Councillor Moyo still ahead by four points. The election will be held on the third of next month, and the final debate on the radio takes place a week earlier. Voters who cannot attend can listen to both on our website.

items.prompt: What was wrong with Tuesday's front page?
items.answer: The cost and the opening date
items.audio:
Good morning, everyone. I asked you to come in early because we have to talk about Tuesday's front page. As most of you know, we reported that the new sports centre would cost eleven million and open in June. Both facts were wrong. The cost is going to be about seventeen million, and the opening is planned for September. Eleven and seventeen sound nothing alike, so it was not a simple misreading. It happened because the figure from last year's draft was used instead of the current one.

I'm not looking for someone to blame. The reporter, Stefan, did what he was told to do, and the desk editor was on holiday. But the system failed, and the system is my responsibility. From today, every number in a story must be checked against a document, not against another article, and the name of the person who checked it will be noted on the page. I know that some of you will find this irritating. A few years ago I would have, too. But I have learned that readers forgive an honest mistake far more easily than a silent correction.

Which brings me to the correction itself. My first idea was to publish a short note on page two, as we usually do. I changed my mind after the mayor's office rang. They were polite, but they pointed out that nearly four hundred people had written to them to complain about the cost. So we are going to run a correction on the front page, in the same place as the original, and also on the website at the top of the story, with a line explaining what changed. This is going to be uncomfortable, but it is the right thing. The online version will be updated by noon, and the printed note appears tomorrow.

Finally, something positive. Despite the mistake, our website had its best week ever, with ninety thousand visitors. The sad part is that the story with the error was the most read. I'd like to think that people come for the news, not for the mistakes, but I am not certain. Anyway, on Friday we have a training session with a data journalist, Ravshan, who will show us how to check statistics quickly. Attendance is not compulsory, but I'd like everyone from the news desk to come. Lunch will be provided, which I'm told is the real reason many of you will attend. Right. Thank you, and please, let's make next week's paper boring in the best possible way: with no corrections at all.
options: The cost and the opening date

items.prompt: How long did the journey to Karakul take the reporter?
items.audio:
For most of us, losing a mobile signal is a minor irritation. For the people of Karakul, a mountain village of about two hundred houses, it was a normal part of life until last month. Our reporter, Bahodir Yunusov, travelled there by a road that took four hours, although the map suggests it should take two, and he found a community still getting used to the idea that a phone can work at home.

The change began when a telecommunications company agreed, after nearly six years of requests, to put an antenna on a hill above the village. Before that, residents who wanted to make a call had to walk up to a rock known as the Telephone Stone, forty minutes uphill, and stand on one leg, according to the local joke. The village teacher, Mrs Rahmonova, told Bahodir that she once learned of her mother's illness two days late because nobody could reach her. She cried when she described it, and admitted that she had not told anyone how she felt until now.

Not everyone is thrilled. The village elder, Mr Abdulloev, who is seventy-eight, worries that young people will spend their evenings staring at screens instead of talking. He has already noticed that three boys who used to play football after school now sit on a wall watching videos. His grandson disagrees, pointing out that he is taking online lessons in English, which would have been impossible before. Mr Abdulloev, to his credit, said that he might be wrong, but that he reserved the right to complain. A shop owner, meanwhile, is delighted. She can now order goods by phone instead of driving down the valley each week, which saves her a day of work and a lot of fuel.

Doctors are also pleased. A nurse who visits the village twice a month can now call a specialist during an examination, and last week she avoided a trip to hospital for a farmer with a badly cut hand. There are still problems. The signal disappears when it snows heavily, and the antenna is powered by solar panels, which do not work well in winter. The company promises a back-up battery by December, but residents have heard promises before. Even so, on the evening Bahodir left, a small crowd had gathered at the village square for no particular reason. They simply wanted, as one man put it, to stand there and hear their phones ring.

items.prompt: What changed at Lucia's daughter's school after the ban?
items.answer: Pupils talked more and argued less online
items.audio:
On this week's episode of Talking Education, hosts Lucia and Hamid discuss whether schools should ban mobile phones completely. Lucia begins by telling a story from her daughter's school, which introduced a ban in January. She expected chaos, but after two weeks the head teacher reported that playground conversation had returned and that the number of arguments over online messages had fallen sharply. Lucia admits that she was sceptical to start with and is now partly convinced.

Hamid takes the opposite side, as he says, on purpose. He argues that a complete ban is the lazy solution. Teachers, he says, should teach children how to use phones sensibly, because they will have phones for the rest of their lives. He mentions a school in the north where pupils use their phones as dictionaries and cameras in science lessons. Lucia replies that she is not against phones in lessons when the teacher decides, only in the corridors and at break. Hamid concedes that this is a reasonable middle position, though he insists that it is not a ban, but a rule, and that the difference matters.

They then discuss research. Lucia has read a study of forty schools which found that results improved slightly after bans, mostly among weaker pupils, while strong pupils hardly changed. Hamid points out that the improvement was small, only about two percent, and that the study was paid for by a company that sells lockers for phones. Lucia laughs and says that this is a fair point she had not noticed. She promises to look for independent evidence and put the links on the website. They agree that the most reliable fact is that nobody really knows yet.

A listener, a teacher named Yusuf, wrote in to say that the real difficulty is parents. Many of them text their children during lessons, and some become angry when the school tries to stop it. His school solved the problem by giving parents the office number and asking them to call that instead. It reduced messages by about half within a month. Hamid says this is the most useful idea he has heard all year. In the end, the hosts do not agree, and they say this is fine. Next week they will talk about whether homework should be abolished, and they would like listeners to send examples of the best and worst homework they ever received. Messages can be sent until Thursday.
options: Pupils talked more and argued less online
There was chaos for two weeks

Lucia begins by telling a story from her daughter's school, which introduced a ban in January. She expected chaos, but after two weeks the head teacher reported that playground conversation had returned and that the number of arguments over online messages had fallen sharply. Lucia admits that she was sceptical to start with and is now partly convinced.

Hamid takes the opposite side, as he says, on purpose. He argues that a complete ban is the lazy solution. Teachers, he says, should teach children how to use phones sensibly, because they will have phones for the rest of their lives. He mentions a school in the north where pupils use their phones as dictionaries and cameras in science lessons. Lucia replies that she is not against phones in lessons when the teacher decides, only in the corridors and at break. Hamid concedes that this is a reasonable middle position, though he insists that it is not a ban, but a rule, and that the difference matters.

They then discuss research. Lucia has read a study of forty schools which found that results improved slightly after bans, mostly among weaker pupils, while strong pupils hardly changed. Hamid points out that the improvement was small, only about two percent, and that the study was paid for by a company that sells lockers for phones. Lucia laughs and says that this is a fair point she had not noticed. She promises to look for independent evidence and put the links on the website. They agree that the most reliable fact is that nobody really knows yet.

A listener, a teacher named Yusuf, wrote in to say that the real difficulty is parents. Many of them text their children during lessons, and some become angry when the school tries to stop it. His school solved the problem by giving parents the office number and asking them to call that instead. It reduced messages by about half within a month. Hamid says this is the most useful idea he has heard all year. In the end, the hosts do not agree, and they say this is fine. Next week they will talk about whether homework should be abolished, and they would like listeners to send examples of the best and worst homework they ever received. Messages can be sent until Thursday.

items.prompt: How did Yusuf's school reduce messages from parents?
items.answer: It asked parents to call the office instead

items.prompt: What is the minimum delay now expected?
items.audio:
Good evening, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome to the departures hall at Istanbul airport. This is an important announcement for all passengers travelling on the Uzbekistan Air flight to Tashkent. We regret to inform you that the flight, which was originally scheduled to leave at nine fifteen, will now depart later than planned. At first, our ground staff believed the delay would be thirteen minutes, but I have just been told that the aircraft arrived from Baku with a technical fault in its landing equipment, so the delay will in fact be thirty minutes at the very least. Please ignore the earlier message on the screens. The new departure time is therefore nine forty five, and we will confirm this again in twenty minutes.

There is also a change of gate. You were originally told to go to gate fourteen, and many of you have already queued there. I am sorry, that gate has now been closed for cleaning. Please make your way to gate forty, which is at the far end of the main corridor, beyond the duty free shops. It takes about ten minutes on foot, so please do not leave it until the last moment. Passengers who need help with wheelchairs or small children should speak to any member of staff in a yellow jacket, and a free buggy service is running every five minutes from the information desk.

Because of the delay, the airline would like to offer every adult passenger a meal voucher. The voucher is worth fifteen euros and may be used in any restaurant on the upper floor, but not in the coffee bars downstairs, which do not accept them. Please note that the voucher cannot be exchanged for cash, and alcohol is not included. Passengers under the age of eighteen will receive a smaller voucher, worth ten euros. If you would like to collect yours, go to the desk next to gate thirty eight, where two colleagues will check your boarding pass. You do not need to show your passport.

Some of you have asked whether the flight might be cancelled altogether. At the moment, we do not expect that, although I must be honest and say that the engineers have not yet finished their inspection. If the problem turns out to be more serious than they think, we will arrange hotel rooms and transport for everyone, and there will be an announcement before ten fifteen. Passengers with a connecting flight from Tashkent to Samarkand have been contacted separately, and a seat has been kept for them on the later evening service, so they should not worry. Those who checked in bags do not need to collect them; your luggage will stay on the aircraft and be loaded as soon as possible.

Finally, may I thank you for your patience. We know that nobody enjoys waiting, especially after a long day, and we sincerely apologise for the inconvenience. Our staff will be happy to answer any further questions at gate forty. Thank you.
items.explain: The speaker corrects the first estimate: at least thirty minutes.

items.prompt: On which day is the museum closed?
items.audio:
Welcome, everyone, to the Ark of Bukhara. My name is Dilnoza, and I will be your guide for the next ninety minutes. Before we go through the gate, a few practical points. Photography is allowed outside, but please do not use flash in the throne room, and the museum on the second level is closed on Mondays, so if you wanted to see the coin collection you will have to come back tomorrow. Toilets are on your left, just before the ticket office, not inside the fortress.

Now, the history. Many guidebooks claim that the fortress is over two thousand years old, and local people like to repeat this. Honestly, I think that is a bit of a romantic exaggeration. Archaeologists have found traces of settlement from that period, but the walls you can see today were mostly rebuilt after a great fire in the sixteenth century, and then again after an attack in eighteen sixty eight. The oldest part still standing is the western tower. I first said it was fourteen metres high, but let me correct myself, it is actually forty metres, which is why the emir's guards could see travellers coming from so far away.

As we walk up the ramp, notice how wide it is. It was built that way not for carts, as visitors often assume, but so that the emir could ride up on horseback with his entire escort. Carts were never allowed inside. Supplies were carried in by hand through a small side door, which is now blocked.

Inside, we will visit the reception hall first. It is a surprisingly modest room, and this is something that disappoints some tourists, who expect gold everywhere. In fact, the emir preferred to impress foreign envoys with silence and waiting. Visitors might stand for several hours before being invited to speak. I find this rather clever, and, frankly, rather cruel. Next to it is the old prison, which was in use until nineteen twenty. We will not go down to the cellar, because the stairs are unsafe, but you can look through the window.

Later we will climb the tower for the view. I should warn you that there are one hundred and ten steps and no lift, so if you have trouble with your knees, there is a bench in the courtyard where you can wait, and my colleague Sardor will sit with you. The climb takes about twenty minutes in total, with a short rest halfway, where there is a small window with a lovely view of the Kalon minaret.

One last thing. Please keep your group together. The courtyards look similar, and last summer a visitor wandered into the staff area and was found two hours later, perfectly happy, eating sweets and drinking tea with the gardeners. If you do get lost, do not panic; just ask anyone wearing a green scarf. Right, shall we begin?
items.explain: The museum is closed on Mondays.

I first said it was fourteen metres high, but let me correct myself, it is actually forty metres, which is why the emir's guards could see travellers coming from so far away.

As we walk up the ramp, notice how wide it is. It was built that way not for carts, as visitors often assume, but so that the emir could ride up on horseback with his entire escort. Carts were never allowed inside. Supplies were carried in by hand through a small side door, which is now blocked.

Inside, we will visit the reception hall first. It is a surprisingly modest room, and this is something that disappoints some tourists, who expect gold everywhere. In fact, the emir preferred to impress foreign envoys with silence and waiting. Visitors might stand for several hours before being invited to speak. I find this rather clever, and, frankly, rather cruel. Next to it is the old prison, which was in use until nineteen twenty. We will not go down to the cellar, because the stairs are unsafe, but you can look through the window.

Later we will climb the tower for the view. I should warn you that there are one hundred and ten steps and no lift, so if you have trouble with your knees, there is a bench in the courtyard where you can wait, and my colleague Sardor will sit with you. The climb takes about twenty minutes in total, with a short rest halfway, where there is a small window with a lovely view of the Kalon minaret.

One last thing. Please keep your group together. The courtyards look similar, and last summer a visitor wandered into the staff area and was found two hours later, perfectly happy, eating sweets and drinking tea with the gardeners. If you do get lost, do not panic; just ask anyone wearing a green scarf. Right, shall we begin?

items.prompt: What did the presenter originally think was the main problem?
items.audio:
Good morning, and welcome to this week's edition of Land and Weather. Today I want to talk about how a changing climate is affecting farming in Central Asia, and I will start with a small confession. When I began researching this programme five years ago, I assumed the main problem would be heat. It turns out that I was only partly right. Heat matters, of course, but what keeps the farmers I interviewed awake at night is water, and above all the timing of water.

Take the example of Bahodir, who grows wheat and apricots near Fergana. His grandfather could predict the first spring melt almost to the week, because the mountain snow always began to disappear in the middle of March. Now it may begin in February, and then a late frost arrives in April and destroys the blossom. Two years ago he lost nearly half of his apricot crop in a single night. He told me he would never plant that variety again, although, to be fair, he changed his mind last year when a new frost resistant tree was offered at a good price.

Scientists at the university in Tashkent have measured the change carefully. According to their figures, the average summer temperature in the region has risen by about one point five degrees in forty years. That sounds small, but they point out that the number of days above forty degrees has doubled, from around ten to around twenty. I should say that the researchers disagree about the cause of the shorter winters, and one professor told me, quite bluntly, that the public discussion is too simple.

So what are farmers doing? Some are switching from cotton to crops that need less water, such as lentils and chickpeas. Others are installing drip irrigation, which can reduce water use by almost a third. The government offers help with the cost, but not for everyone. Only farms smaller than ten hectares qualify, which frustrates owners of larger farms who say they are the ones who waste the most water and need the change most.

There is also a quieter, older answer. Women in the village of Qarshi still dry vegetables and fruit in the sun and store them for winter, a tradition that many young people had abandoned. A cooperative there now sells these products in the capital, and its manager, Gulnora, told me that profits have grown fourfold since last year. She is not worried about the future, she said, because people have always adapted. I am less sure. Adaptation costs money, and small farmers rarely have much.

My own view is that we need honest planning rather than panic. After the news, we will hear from an engineer who believes the old canals can be repaired cheaply. Stay with us.
items.explain: He assumed heat; farmers actually worry about water timing.

items.prompt: Which room is Marcus really in?
items.audio:
Marcus calls the reception desk of a hotel in Samarkand at about eleven at night. He explains that he is in room three hundred and twelve, and then corrects himself: it is room two hundred and thirteen, because he had read the number on his key card the wrong way round. His problem is noise. A wedding party is taking place in the garden below his window, and the music, he says, has been going since eight. The receptionist, a young woman called Madina, apologises and explains that the hotel did mention the wedding in an email sent last week. Marcus answers that he never received any email, and in any case a mention is not the same as a warning, because he specifically booked a quiet room facing the street, not the garden.

Madina checks the system and agrees that his booking does say street side. She admits that the hotel moved him without asking, because a pipe burst on the third floor on Tuesday. Marcus is not satisfied. He says somebody should have told him at check in, and he adds that he is not angry with her personally, only with the management. Madina offers to move him to a room on the fourth floor at the front of the building. Marcus hesitates, because he has an early meeting at seven and does not want to pack at midnight. He suggests that she send someone to help with the bags. She says that a porter will be there in ten minutes, but unfortunately the new room has a double bed, and he booked twin beds, because he is travelling with a colleague, Hamid, who is already asleep.

After some discussion they find a compromise. Instead of moving, Marcus will stay where he is, and the hotel will give him a refund for one night, which is ninety dollars, though he first asks for a hundred and fifty. Madina says she can only authorise one night, because larger sums need the manager, who is away until morning. In addition, she promises to ask the wedding organisers to turn the music down at half past eleven rather than at one in the morning, which is what the licence allows. Marcus is doubtful that this will work, but he thanks her.

Before hanging up, he asks about breakfast. The restaurant normally opens at seven thirty, which is too late for him, so Madina agrees to leave a packed breakfast at the desk. It will contain bread, boiled eggs, fruit and tea in a flask, but, she warns, no coffee, since the machine is broken. Marcus laughs and says that after tonight he can live without it.

The next morning, he finds that the music did stop at half past eleven, and he sleeps rather well. At the desk, he leaves a polite note for the manager, praising Madina and complaining only about the lack of information. He says he would stay again, but only if the hotel promises to tell guests about events in advance.
items.explain: He corrects himself to room two hundred and thirteen.

items.prompt: What was Aziza's original profession?
items.audio:
In a recent interview, the conservationist Aziza Karimova described her fifteen years working to protect snow leopards in the Tien Shan mountains. The interviewer began by asking whether she had always wanted this career. Aziza laughed and said no; she trained as an accountant, and only changed direction after a holiday trek when she saw fresh paw prints beside a frozen stream. She admitted that she was terrified at the time, though she later realised the animal was probably more afraid of her.

Asked about the biggest threat to the species, she did not name hunting, as most people expect. Poaching still exists, she said, but its effect has fallen sharply over the past decade. The real danger now is conflict with herders. When a leopard kills sheep, the family loses perhaps a month's income, and understandably they take revenge. Her organisation therefore pays compensation, but she is quick to say that she does not like the word. She prefers to call it insurance, because the herders contribute a small amount each year, and the fund covers their losses. Since the scheme began, retaliatory killings in the valley have dropped from about twelve a year to one or two.

The interviewer suggested that tourism might harm the animals. Aziza disagreed, at least partly. Visitors, she explained, bring money that pays the rangers, and a living leopard is worth more to a village than a dead one. However, she insisted on strict limits: no more than eight tourists at a time, no drones, and nobody closer than two hundred metres to a den. She once refused a famous film company permission to film because they wanted to use a helicopter, even though they offered a large donation. Some colleagues thought she was foolish. She does not regret it.

On the subject of numbers, she was cautious. Camera traps suggest there are about thirty five adult animals in her region, not fifty, which was the figure in an old report. She stressed that this earlier estimate was based on guesswork, and that better counting does not mean the population is falling; it simply means they now know more. Still, she would not call the situation safe.

Towards the end, the interviewer asked about her hopes. Aziza said that she does not expect to see a dramatic change in her lifetime, but she believes in small victories. Last winter, a female leopard with two cubs was photographed on a ridge where none had been seen for twenty years. She keeps the photograph above her desk. And her advice for young people? Do not wait for the perfect job, she said; volunteer, learn to read the landscape, and be patient, because conservation moves at the speed of a mountain, not of a news report.
items.explain: She trained as an accountant.

In a recent interview, the conservationist Aziza Karimova described her fifteen years working to protect snow leopards in the Tien Shan mountains. The interviewer began by asking whether she had always wanted this career. Aziza laughed and said no; she trained as an accountant, and only changed direction after a holiday trek when she saw fresh paw prints beside a frozen stream. She admitted that she was terrified at the time, though she later realised the animal was probably more afraid of her.

Asked about the biggest threat to the species, she did not name hunting, as most people expect. Poaching still exists, she said, but its effect has fallen sharply over the past decade. The real danger now is conflict with herders. When a leopard kills sheep, the family loses perhaps a month's income, and understandably they take revenge. Her organisation therefore pays compensation, but she is quick to say that she does not like the word. She prefers to call it insurance, because the herders contribute a small amount each year, and the fund covers their losses. Since the scheme began, retaliatory killings in the valley have dropped from about twelve a year to one or two.

The interviewer suggested that tourism might harm the animals. Aziza disagreed, at least partly. Visitors, she explained, bring money that pays the rangers, and a living leopard is worth more to a village than a dead one. However, she insisted on strict limits: no more than eight tourists at a time, no drones, and nobody closer than two hundred metres to a den. She once refused a famous film company permission to film because they wanted to use a helicopter, even though they offered a large donation. Some colleagues thought she was foolish. She does not regret it.

On the subject of numbers, she was cautious. Camera traps suggest there are about thirty five adult animals in her region, not fifty, which was the figure in an old report. She stressed that this earlier estimate was based on guesswork, and that better counting does not mean the population is falling; it simply means they now know more. Still, she would not call the situation safe.

Towards the end, the interviewer asked about her hopes. Aziza said that she does not expect to see a dramatic change in her lifetime, but she believes in small victories. Last winter, a female leopard with two cubs was photographed on a ridge where none had been seen for twenty years. She keeps the photograph above her desk. And her advice for young people? Do not wait for the perfect job, she said; volunteer, learn to read the landscape, and be patient, because conservation moves at the speed of a mountain, not of a news report.

They came at the wrong time of year.

items.prompt: What time does the opening ceremony really begin?
items.audio:
Welcome to the programme announcement for this year's Silk and Spice Festival in Margilan, which opens on Friday and runs for four days. I will go through the main events, and I should start with a correction to the printed leaflet. It says that the opening ceremony begins at six o'clock, but it will in fact begin at seven, because the mayor has to attend a council meeting first. Please tell your friends.

Friday evening begins with a parade from the old bazaar to the central square, led by drummers and dancers in traditional costume. Do not bring cars; the roads are closed from five. Then, at half past eight, the folk singer Zulfiya Rahimova will perform on the main stage. Tickets for this concert are free, but you must collect them in advance from the tourist office, and only two per person are allowed.

On Saturday, the festival becomes more practical. There are workshops all day: silk weaving at ten, pottery at noon, and cooking at three. The cooking class has been very popular, so it has moved from the small kitchen to the school hall, which holds sixty people instead of twenty. Each workshop costs fifteen thousand sums, except weaving, which is thirty thousand because of the materials. Children under twelve may join free if accompanied by an adult. In the evening there is a film screening in the park. The organisers originally planned an outdoor showing, but the forecast promises rain, so it will be inside the cultural centre, which means space is limited and you should arrive early.

Sunday is the day for the food market, where over eighty stalls will sell sweets, spices, bread and dried fruit. I personally recommend the stall near the fountain which sells honey from the Fergana hills; it was the best I have tasted. Vegetarians should know that the plov competition at noon is meat based, though there will be a vegetable version later, around two. The winner of the competition receives a golden spoon and a year of free flour from a local mill, which, to be honest, seems like a very practical prize.

The final day, Monday, is quieter, with a poetry reading in the morning and a closing concert at five. Many visitors leave early on Monday, which I think is a mistake, because the closing concert is often the highlight. Last year the organisers surprised everyone with a fireworks display that lasted twenty minutes.

A few practical notes. Parking is available behind the railway station, with a free shuttle bus every fifteen minutes. Toilets and first aid points are marked on the map, and a lost property office will be open in the library. Please bring a reusable bottle; the organisers have installed free water points to reduce plastic waste, and single use bottles will not be sold. We look forward to seeing you.
items.explain: The leaflet says six, but it begins at seven.

items.prompt: What is the new departure time of the morning train?
items.audio:
Attention please, passengers of the fast railway line between Tashkent and Samarkand. From the first of December the timetable will change, and I would like to explain exactly what this means for you. The morning train that used to leave at seven fifty will now leave at seven fifteen, so it will be thirty five minutes earlier. I know that sounds strange, because most people think a new timetable means later trains. The reason is that the company wants to avoid the morning rush at the main station. Please do not confuse this with the evening train, which will go the opposite way: it used to leave at five fifteen but will now depart at five fifty.

The journey itself will become quicker. The old train took two hours and ten minutes, but after the track repairs near Jizzakh are finished, it will take only one hour and fifty minutes. At the moment, those repairs are not complete, so for the first three weeks the trains will run slowly and the journey will take the old time. I mention this because the website states that the faster service starts immediately, and that is wrong. The company has promised to correct the page, though so far it hasn't.

Ticket prices are changing too. A standard seat will cost one hundred and ten thousand sums, an increase of ten thousand. First class remains the same, at one hundred and sixty thousand. However, if you buy your ticket at least fourteen days in advance, you can pay only ninety thousand, which is a bargain. Students and pensioners get a discount of twenty per cent on all tickets, but not on those bought on the train itself. Children under five travel free, provided that they sit on an adult's knee; if they need their own seat, you must buy a half price ticket.

There are also changes to the stations. The old waiting room at Tashkent South is being rebuilt, so passengers should use the temporary hall behind the car park, which is about two hundred metres from the platform. Luggage lockers will not be available until February. On the positive side, the new cafe on platform two will open next week and will serve hot food from six in the morning. Smoking will be forbidden everywhere on the platforms, not only inside buildings, and the fine for ignoring this rule is two hundred thousand sums.

Finally, a word about delays. During last winter, nearly one train in five arrived late, mostly because of snow and ice on the track. This year the company has bought new snow clearing machines, and it expects the figure to fall to one in twenty. I personally am not sure that this is realistic, since the weather is difficult to predict. If your train is more than half an hour late, you may ask for a refund of half the ticket price at any ticket office. For information, call the helpline, or visit the station. Thank you for listening, and have a pleasant journey.
items.explain: It moves from seven fifty to seven fifteen.

items.prompt: Where did the speaker move to study?
items.audio:
Thank you all for coming. Tonight I want to talk about culture shock, a subject I know a little about, because three years ago I moved from Namangan to Glasgow to study for a master's degree. When I tell people this, they often expect a story about weather or food. Those things were certainly new, but what surprised me most were small invisible rules, the things nobody explains because everyone already knows them.

Let me give you an example. In my first week, I was invited to dinner by a classmate called Fiona. In Uzbekistan, when you are a guest, you refuse a second helping once or twice, and the host insists until you finally accept. So when Fiona asked whether I would like some more, I said no, thank you, expecting her to ask again. She did not. She simply cleared the plates, and I went home hungry. Only later did I understand that in Scotland, a polite no usually means no. It was a small thing, but I remember feeling foolish and homesick.

Many researchers describe culture shock as a curve with four stages. First comes the honeymoon, when everything seems exciting. Then comes frustration, which is the hardest stage, and for me it began after about six weeks, not three months, as the textbooks say. After that there is adjustment, and finally acceptance. I should add that the stages are not a staircase. You can fall back from acceptance to frustration on a bad day, for instance when you cannot find the right word in a seminar and everybody waits politely.

What helped me? First, I stopped comparing. At the start I kept saying that in my country things were done better, and my friends quickly became tired of it. Second, I joined a walking club, mostly by accident, because I thought it was a chess club. The members were retired teachers, and they were kind, patient and very funny. Third, and this surprised me, I cooked more. Making plov in my tiny kitchen gave me a sense of home that no phone call to my mother could give.

There is also reverse culture shock, which almost nobody warns you about. When I returned to Namangan for the summer, I noticed that I now found the traffic loud and the questions about my salary rather personal. My cousin laughed and said I had become a foreigner. That hurt a little, but it was also true, and I think it is an honest result of living between two cultures.

So what is my advice to those of you who are about to travel? Be curious, not judgmental. Accept that you will make mistakes. And do not wait for the feeling to disappear, because it never completely does; it simply changes into something more interesting. Now, I would be happy to take your questions.
items.explain: From Namangan to Glasgow.

items.prompt: Why might some campers avoid the pitches near the lake?
items.answer: The ground gets soft and wet after rain.
items.audio:
Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to Lake Aydar campsite. My name is Rustam, and I am the warden here until the end of the season. I will keep this short, because I know you want to put up your tents before it gets dark, but there are several rules that really matter.

First, check in. Your pitch numbers are on the card I gave you at the gate. A few of you have number twelve and number twenty, so please check carefully, since these are at opposite ends of the site. Pitches under fifteen are near the lake, and they are the most popular, but they are also the wettest after rain, because the ground is soft. If you prefer dry ground, I suggest the upper field, which has fewer trees but better views of the mountains.

Fires are the most serious issue. You may light fires only in the metal rings provided, never on the grass, and never after ten at night. Last summer a family ignored this and set fire to a small area of forest. Nobody was hurt, thankfully, but we lost around two hectares. Firewood is sold at the shop for five thousand sums a bundle; please do not cut branches from living trees, even if you see others doing it. Gas stoves are permitted anywhere, except inside tents.

Water comes from the tap beside the shower block, and it is perfectly safe to drink. The showers are hot between six and nine in the morning and again from five to eight in the evening, but the hot water is limited, so please keep it short. Many people expect the toilets to be far away, but the nearest ones are only fifty metres from the lower pitches. Do not wash dishes in the lake; there is a sink behind the shop.

About animals. You may see foxes, and they will try to steal food. Keep everything in sealed boxes or in your car. Wild boar are very rare, but if you meet one, stay calm and walk away slowly. Do not feed anything; I know it is tempting, but human food makes animals dependent. Dogs are welcome, but must be on a lead at all times, because the sheep from the neighbouring farm sometimes wander in.

Quiet time begins at eleven, not ten, as the sign at the gate says. That sign is old and I have not had time to replace it. Music is allowed before then, but only at a low volume.

If you want activities, I run a guided walk to the waterfall every morning at eight; it takes three hours, and it is free. items.prompt: Where was the large carpet made?
items.audio:
Welcome to the National Textile Museum. You are now standing in the entrance hall, beneath the great chandelier. Please press the green button on your device to pause this recording at any time, and press the red one to repeat. The tour has twelve stops and lasts about fifty minutes, but you are free to skip any stop that does not interest you.

Let us begin with the large carpet on the wall to your right. Many visitors assume it was made in Persia, because of its colours and pattern. In fact, it was woven in Bukhara around eighteen forty by a group of about twenty women, and it took them almost three years. The deep red dye comes from the roots of a plant called madder, while the blue comes from indigo imported from India. Please do not touch the carpet, however tempting. The oils on our hands damage the fibres, and the museum has had to replace a section twice.

Now walk through the arch to the second room, where silk is the main subject. Notice the small screen showing a silkworm in action. A single cocoon can produce about one thousand metres of thread, though it takes many cocoons to make one scarf. Some historians believe that silk reached the region in the second century, others say much later, and the truth is that nobody knows for certain. I personally find the uncertainty rather charming.

In the glass case on your left you will see a child's coat from the early twentieth century. It looks plain, but look closely at the collar. The embroidery contains tiny symbols meant to protect the wearer from illness, and the curator, Professor Nodira Yusupova, spent six months trying to read them. She is still not sure about two of the symbols. Before you move on, you may notice that the coat is bigger than you expected. Children at that time were not larger than today, but the coat was made for a ceremony, not for everyday use, and the family wanted the child to grow into it.

On the first floor, there is a temporary exhibition about modern designers. If you have a general ticket, you can visit it for free, but the audio guide does not cover it; instead, scan the code on the wall. The cafe next to it serves tea and pastries, but I should warn you that it closes at four, an hour earlier than the museum itself, which stays open until five.

The last stop is the workshop. On weekdays, you can watch a weaver at work, and on Saturdays visitors may try the loom themselves for ten minutes. Sundays are reserved for school groups, so the workshop is closed to individuals. Before you leave, please return your device to the desk by the main door, and thank you for visiting. We hope that you will come back soon.
items.explain: Many visitors wrongly assume Persia.

items.prompt: Which bin is for glass?
items.audio:
Good evening, and thank you for tuning in to the local news from Chirchik. The city council announced today the details of a new recycling scheme that will begin in the spring. The deputy mayor, Elyor Tursunov, presented the plan at a press conference this morning, and I will summarise the main points.

From the first of April, each household will receive three coloured bins: blue for paper and cardboard, yellow for plastic and metal, and green for glass. Food waste will not be collected separately for now, although the council says that may change in two years. Residents will not be charged for the bins, but if one is lost or damaged, the replacement costs forty thousand sums. Collection days will be Tuesday for blue, Thursday for yellow, and every second Saturday for green. Mister Tursunov at first said Wednesday for the yellow bins, but he corrected himself after a colleague whispered in his ear. It will be Thursday.

Why is the council doing this? At the moment, only about eight per cent of the city's rubbish is recycled, while the national average is around eighteen. The landfill outside the city is nearly full, and a new one would cost the equivalent of six million dollars. The deputy mayor said it would be cheaper to teach people to sort their rubbish. Not everyone agrees. A councillor from the opposition, Malika Sodiqova, argued that the plan ignores apartment blocks, where there is no room for three bins in each flat. The deputy mayor answered that blocks will have shared containers in the yard, but he admitted that the details are not yet finalised.

There is also a financial incentive. Families who recycle regularly will receive a discount on their water bill, up to ten per cent, based on the weight of the sorted material measured by the collection lorries. Critics say this will encourage people to put heavy, useless items in the bins, such as stones, and the council promises that inspectors will check random bins, with fines of up to two hundred thousand sums for cheating.

Schools will take part in the project too. Every pupil will have a short lesson about waste, and the best class in each district will win a trip to the mountains in June. Local businesses are also asked to join in. A supermarket chain has already agreed to stop using plastic bags and will give a small discount to customers who bring their own, which pleased the environmental groups, though one activist said it was too little, too late.

Finally, the council will hold three public meetings, on the sixth, the thirteenth, and the twentieth of March, in the town hall at seven in the evening. Residents who cannot attend can send questions by telephone or through the council's website. The deputy mayor said he is confident that the scheme will work, but he also said that, to be honest, the first months will be chaotic. We will keep you informed. And now, the weather.
items.explain: Green is for glass.

items.prompt: How long is the crossing in calm weather?
items.audio:
Good morning, everybody, and welcome aboard. I am Captain Beatriz Santos, and with me is my assistant, Tomas. Today we are sailing to Puffin Island, which is about nine miles from the harbour, and the crossing will take roughly forty minutes if the sea remains calm. I should mention that the forecast has changed since last night. Yesterday they promised sunshine all day, but this morning they are talking about wind in the afternoon, so we will return an hour earlier than printed on your tickets, at three instead of four.

Before we leave, some safety information. Life jackets are under the seats, and you should wear one on the upper deck, though it is optional inside the cabin. If you feel seasick, sit near the middle of the boat and look at the horizon. We also have tablets, but they must be taken before we leave, not after you feel ill, so please see Tomas now if you want one. Children must stay with an adult at all times. No smoking is allowed anywhere on the boat, including the open deck, even though some people think the rule only applies indoors.

Now, about the island itself. It is a protected nature reserve, home to about four thousand pairs of puffins in summer, and in July also some seals. We will be allowed to land for ninety minutes, and then follow a single path marked with white stones. Please stay on the path. The birds nest in burrows under the grass, and one careless step can destroy a nest. I have seen it happen, and it is not a pleasant sight. Do not bring food onto the island, because gulls are clever and will steal it, and a hungry gull can be aggressive. Drinks in sealed bottles are fine.

Photography is encouraged, but flash is not, and drones are completely forbidden. If you wish to sit and watch the birds, there is a wooden hide halfway along the path, which holds about twelve people, so do not stay for longer than ten minutes if others are waiting. Binoculars can be borrowed from Tomas for a deposit of twenty thousand sums, which you will get back when you return them.

A word about the weather: if it becomes too windy, I may decide not to land at all. In that case, we will sail around the island and you will receive a refund of thirty per cent. Please don't be disappointed with me; I would rather disappoint you than risk your safety. It happened three times last year, and each time the passengers eventually agreed I had been right.

Finally, there is a small cafe on the lower deck, but the coffee machine is out of order today, so only tea and cold drinks are available. The toilets are at the back, and I ask you to flush gently. Tomas will now hand out the life jackets, and we will leave in five minutes. Enjoy the trip.
items.explain: Nine is the distance in miles, ninety the landing time.

items.audio:
Hello again, everyone, and welcome back to the channel. This week's video is about my four days in the Kyzylkum desert, where I stayed at a yurt camp near Aydarkul. Before I start, a confession: I nearly cancelled the trip. A week before departure my friend Sanjar, who was supposed to come with me, broke his ankle playing football, and I was ready to give up. But my sister told me I would regret it, and as usual she was right.

We began in Bukhara and drove for about five hours. The driver, a cheerful man called Ravshan, had warned me that the last stretch would be rough, and he was not exaggerating. The road became a track, and the track became sand. When we arrived, it was already half past six, and the sunset over the dunes was the most beautiful thing I have seen this year. I am not usually emotional about landscapes, but I actually went quiet.

The camp has eight yurts, each with space for four people. Mine was number five, and it was simple but comfortable: thick felt walls, colourful rugs, and mattresses on the floor. Some travellers online complained about the cold at night, and honestly they were right. In October the temperature drops almost to zero, so bring warm socks. There is no electricity in the yurts, only a few solar lamps, so charge your phone before you arrive. There is a signal near the main tent, but it is weak.

The food was a pleasant surprise. The owners, an elderly couple called Karim and Oysha, cooked on an open fire. For dinner we had shurpa and fresh bread, and I was told that the lamb came from their own herd. Breakfast was fried eggs and fruit. I expected the water to be limited, but there was plenty, though showering with a bucket takes some practice.

On the second day, we rode camels for about two hours. I was nervous, because I had heard they smell and bite, but my camel, called Gulya, was gentle. After a while, I found the rhythm quite relaxing, though my legs were sore the next morning. At night, the guide took us out to look at the stars. With no city lights, you can see the whole Milky Way, and he showed us a constellation that locals use to find north. I tried to photograph it, but my phone could not manage it, so you will have to trust me.

Would I go back? Absolutely, but I would choose spring, when the desert is green and flowers appear for a few weeks. The camp costs about forty dollars a night, including all meals, which I think is excellent value. I will put the contact details in the description below. If you enjoyed this video, please like it, subscribe, and tell me where I should travel next.

The food was a pleasant surprise. The owners, an elderly couple called Karim and Oysha, cooked on an open fire. For dinner we had shurpa and fresh bread, and I was told that the lamb came from their own herd. Breakfast was fried eggs and fruit. I expected the water to be limited, but there was plenty, though showering with a bucket takes some practice.

On the second day, we rode camels for about two hours. I was nervous, because I had heard they smell and bite, but my camel, called Gulya, was gentle. After a while, I found the rhythm quite relaxing, though my legs were sore the next morning. At night, the guide took us out to look at the stars. With no city lights, you can see the whole Milky Way, and he showed us a constellation that locals use to find north. I tried to photograph it, but my phone could not manage it, so you will have to trust me.

Would I go back? Absolutely, but I would choose spring, when the desert is green and flowers appear for a few weeks. The camp costs about forty dollars a night, including all meals, which I think is excellent value. I will put the contact details in the description below. If you enjoyed this video, please like it, subscribe, and tell me where I should travel next.

items.prompt: Why did Shirin advise against the southern route?
items.answer: The pass is very high and may have snow.
items.audio:
Last Tuesday, Oliver, a cycling enthusiast from Manchester, phoned the tourist information centre in Tashkent to ask about a week long route through the Fergana Valley. The adviser, Shirin, explained that there were two possible routes. The northern route is about three hundred and fifty kilometres and goes mainly along quiet roads, while the southern route is only two hundred and fifty, but it includes a long climb over a mountain pass. Oliver said that he preferred the shorter one, because he had been ill in the spring and was not fully fit. Shirin advised him to think again. The pass, she said, reaches over two thousand metres, and in October there can already be snow. She added that she herself cycled it last year and had to walk the last stretch.

Oliver then asked about accommodation. Shirin told him that the small guesthouses in the valley were cheap, around twenty dollars a night with breakfast, but they were often full in autumn because of the harvest festival. He should book at least two weeks ahead. Hotels in the cities, on the other hand, were more expensive, and she did not recommend them because they were far from the route. Oliver asked whether he could bring his own bicycle on the plane. She said yes, but he should check with the airline about the fee, which could be as high as a hundred dollars, and that renting a good bicycle locally would cost only ten dollars a day, which would be cheaper overall for a week. However, she warned that rental bikes were not always in good condition, and he should inspect the brakes carefully.

They moved on to safety. Shirin said that drivers in the valley were generally patient but unpredictable, and that cyclists should wear bright clothing. Dogs were more of a problem than traffic, she said, and she suggested that he should never run away from them, but slow down and talk calmly. Oliver laughed and said he had been bitten once in Greece. Shirin laughed too, though she added that a rabies injection before the trip was a sensible idea, and that the clinic in the centre of Tashkent offered it for a reasonable price.

On the matter of food, she recommended that he carry snacks, since the villages could be forty kilometres apart, and that he drink more water than he thought necessary, at least three litres a day. Oliver asked about the best month. She said September, when the weather is warm but not hot, and the fruit is at its best, although he would have to cope with crowds in the markets, which could be a pleasure rather than a problem.

By the end of the call, Oliver had changed his mind. He decided to take the northern route, rent a bicycle in Kokand, and set off on the fourth of October. Shirin promised to email a map, a list of guesthouses, and the number of a mechanic in Andijan, who speaks English and is, she said, a very good friend of hers. Oliver thanked her warmly and said that he was already looking forward to the journey.
options: The pass is very high and may have snow.

items.prompt: Why has the spice bazaar visit been replaced?
items.audio:
Hello, food lovers, and welcome to the Old Town night market tour. I am Kamila, and for the next two hours I will take you through the streets where the best street food in the city is made. Before we set off, let me explain the plan, because it has changed slightly. The original programme included a visit to the spice bazaar, but the owners are renovating, so we will go instead to a family bakery, which, I promise, is better.

Our first stop is a small stall that sells samsa. Many visitors think samsa is a pastry with meat, and this is partly true, but tonight I want you to try the pumpkin version as well. The baker, Uncle Habib, has been making them for forty years in a clay oven, and he told me once that the secret is not the filling, but the temperature of the oven. Please wait until I tell you before you bite. They are very hot, and last month a tourist burned his tongue, and was unhappy for the rest of the evening.

Next, we cross the road to the tea house. There is a custom here that you may find unusual. When the host pours your tea, he fills the cup only half full. This is not stinginess. It is a sign of respect, because it means he will come back to your table many times and give you hot tea. A full cup grows cold, and a cold cup is considered rude. If you want no more tea, place your hand over the cup, or turn it upside down.

After this, we will walk to the dessert street. I want to warn you that some of the sweets are very sweet, much sweeter than in Europe. If you do not like sugar, try the sour plum drink instead. A word about the market rules: bargaining is expected for souvenirs, but never for food, and you should never touch fruit before you have asked. It is considered impolite. Most stallholders accept cash only, so make sure you have enough small notes. Cards are rarely accepted, and the nearest cash machine is ten minutes away.

At the end of the tour, we will have dinner at a courtyard restaurant. The price is included, and the meal has five courses. items.prompt: Why will the welcome talk start later than printed?
items.audio:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the open day at Westbridge University. My name is Dilnoza Karimova, and I will be your guide until lunchtime. First, a quick change to the printed programme. The leaflet says the welcome talk begins at half past nine, but because of a delay with the coaches it will start at ten thirty instead, so you have a little time for coffee. The talk about engineering has been moved to room fifteen, not room fifty, which is in a completely different building, so please check the signs carefully.

Many of you have asked about fees. For students from this country the tuition is nine thousand pounds a year, but there is a bursary for anyone whose family income is below twenty-five thousand. I should add that the bursary is not automatic. You have to apply before the first of March, and last year several excellent candidates missed it because they thought it was included. Accommodation is guaranteed for first-year students, although I have to be honest, the older halls are noisy, and I personally would recommend the new building by the river, even though it costs about forty pounds more per week.

Now, about the courses. I know that some of you came expecting to see the law department, but unfortunately it is closed today because of building work, so you will only be able to meet its staff at the lunch in the main hall. Medicine is not offered here at all, whatever the website might suggest. The old page was out of date, and we are trying to remove it. On the other hand, our psychology course has just been ranked among the top five in the country, which surprised even us.

When I was a student here, I nearly left after the first term. I had chosen economics because my father wanted me to, and I found the lectures dull. A tutor persuaded me to switch to geography, and that decision changed my life. So my advice is simple: do not choose a course only because it sounds impressive. Visit the lectures, talk to current students, and ask the awkward questions. There are twelve student ambassadors in red jackets around the campus, and they will answer anything honestly, even about the food, which, I admit, is not our greatest strength.

Finally, the library tour leaves at noon from the front steps, and the last bus back to the station departs at four forty-five, not five o'clock as it did in previous years. Enjoy your day.

items.prompt: Why did Rustam's card stop working?
items.answer: The bank's security system blocked it
items.audio:
Rustam calls his bank on a Monday morning because his debit card has stopped working in shops. The adviser, whose name is Helen, greets him politely and asks him to confirm his date of birth and the first line of his address. Rustam explains that the card was declined twice at a supermarket on Saturday, which was embarrassing, because he had a full basket and a queue of people behind him.

Helen checks the account and tells him that the card was blocked by the security system. Someone tried to use the number to buy electronics in another country, so the bank froze it automatically. She says that Rustam does not need to worry, because no money has left the account. Rustam is relieved, but he asks how long a replacement will take. Helen first says that it will arrive in fifteen working days, then corrects herself quickly, saying five working days. She apologises and explains that fifteen is the time for cards sent abroad. In the meantime, he can use the mobile app to pay with his phone, which does not need the physical card.

Then Rustam asks about something different. He has been saving for a deposit on a small flat and wonders whether there is a better account than his current one. Helen suggests a savings account with an interest rate of two and a half percent, not twenty-five, as Rustam jokes. The catch is that he cannot take out money more than twice a year without losing the interest for that month. Rustam says that this is not a problem, because he never touches his savings, except in a real emergency. Helen also mentions a fixed-rate account with a higher rate, but she does not recommend it for him, since the money would be locked for three years, and he hopes to buy a flat within two.

Before ending the call, Rustam asks about fees. Helen says transfers within the country are free, and so are cash withdrawals from the bank's own machines. Transfers abroad cost a small fee, apart from those to countries in the same currency zone, which are also free. Rustam thanks her, but he says that he is still not sure about moving his savings today, and he will think about it over the weekend. Helen says that is perfectly sensible and that the offer will remain open until the end of the month. She finishes by reminding him to change his online password, because the attempted fraud suggests that his details may have been leaked from a shop, and to call back if anything looks strange on his statement.
options: The bank's security system blocked it
There was no money in the account

items.prompt: The savings interest rate is two and a ___ percent.
items.audio:
Rustam calls his bank on a Monday morning because his debit card has stopped working in shops. The adviser, whose name is Helen, greets him politely and asks him to confirm his date of birth and the first line of his address. Rustam explains that the card was declined twice at a supermarket on Saturday, which was embarrassing, because he had a full basket and a queue of people behind him.

Helen checks the account and tells him that the card was blocked by the security system. Someone tried to use the number to buy electronics in another country, so the bank froze it automatically. She says that Rustam does not need to worry, because no money has left the account. Rustam is relieved, but he asks how long a replacement will take. Helen first says that it will arrive in fifteen working days, then corrects herself quickly, saying five working days. She apologises and explains that fifteen is the time for cards sent abroad. In the meantime, he can use the mobile app to pay with his phone, which does not need the physical card.

Then Rustam asks about something different. He has been saving for a deposit on a small flat and wonders whether there is a better account than his current one. Helen suggests a savings account with an interest rate of two and a half percent, not twenty-five, as Rustam jokes. Helen says that is perfectly sensible and that the offer will remain open until the end of the month. items.prompt: What happened to the lecturer in her first year?
items.answer: She ran out of money early
items.audio:
Good afternoon. Today I want to talk about something that most of you will have to face very soon, namely how to manage your money when you live away from home for the first time. I will not pretend that I always did it well. In my first year I spent nearly my whole loan in the first two months, and I had to ask my aunt for help, which I still remember with embarrassment.

The method I would like to explain is called the fifty, thirty, twenty rule. Fifty percent of your income goes on needs, such as rent, food and transport. Thirty percent is for wants, meaning entertainment, clothes and travel. The remaining twenty percent is for savings or paying off debts. Some of you will say that it is impossible when rent alone takes sixty percent. I agree, and that is the first lesson, a rule is only a starting point. If your needs are higher, you should reduce the wants rather than the savings, even if that feels unfair.

The second idea is to track your spending for one month. Do not change anything at first, just write it down. Most people are shocked. One student I taught calculated that she was paying thirteen pounds a month for subscriptions she had forgotten about, and she cancelled them the same evening. Another found that coffee on the way to lectures cost him about thirty pounds a month, which is not a fortune, but over a year it adds up to a good holiday. I am not saying that you must give up coffee. I am saying that you should choose it consciously.

Third, build an emergency fund. The usual advice is to save three months of expenses, but for a student that is unrealistic, so I suggest a smaller target of five hundred pounds. That is enough to cover a broken laptop or an unexpected train ticket home. Keep it in a separate account, so you are not tempted to touch it.

Now, a common mistake. Many people believe that using a credit card is always dangerous. It is not, if you pay off the whole balance every month. The danger is paying only the minimum, because the interest can reach twenty-five percent a year. On the other hand, I would not advise any of you to take a payday loan under any circumstances. Those have no exceptions in my book.

Last week a student asked me whether budgeting makes life boring. My answer is the opposite. When you know exactly how much you can spend, you enjoy spending it without guilt. Next week we will look at investing, but I warn you, I will be sceptical about anything that promises quick profits. Please read the first two chapters before then.
options: She ran out of money early

items.prompt: How many times did Aziza apply for scholarships?
items.audio:
Today in our education programme we meet Aziza Nazarova, who has just won a full scholarship to study marine biology in Scotland. The presenter begins by congratulating her and asking how she is feeling. Aziza laughs and says that she is still in shock, because she did not expect to win at all. She had applied three times. The first two applications were rejected, and she admits that after the second she nearly gave up.

The presenter asks what changed the third time. Aziza explains that in the first year she wrote a very general essay about loving the sea, which, as she now understands, was exactly what everyone else wrote. In the second year her grades were not high enough, because she had spent too much time on volunteering. The third time she combined the two, using her volunteer work cleaning beaches as evidence of a long-term commitment, and she raised her marks to ninety-two percent. She says that the interview panel asked her more about the beaches than about her exam results.

The presenter then asks about money, because many listeners worry that scholarships are only for the very rich or the very clever. Aziza disagrees. Her family is not wealthy. Her father drives a taxi and her mother works in a school canteen, and the scholarship covers tuition, accommodation and a monthly allowance of eight hundred pounds. She stresses, however, that it does not cover flights, so she had to raise two thousand pounds herself. A local company helped, and neighbours organised a charity concert, which, she says, moved her to tears.

When asked about the hardest part, Aziza does not mention the application. It was the waiting. For six weeks after the interview she checked her email every hour, and she says her mother told her to stop, but she could not. She also tells a funny story about the day the news arrived. She was in the middle of a chemistry lesson, her phone buzzed, and the teacher, who had banned phones, asked her to leave. Outside, she read the message and screamed so loudly that the whole corridor heard.

Finally, the presenter asks for advice. Aziza says three things. First, apply early, because the deadline is not a friend. Second, ask someone to read your essay who will tell you the truth, not just praise. Third, never think that a rejection means you are not good enough. In her case, she says, the rejections were the best teachers she ever had. The presenter thanks her, and Aziza leaves for the airport next month, though she is already packing.

items.prompt: What problem is there when they arrive?
items.audio:
Zilola and her friend Mark arrive at a small block of flats near the park at four o'clock, and the agent, a young man called Peter, is already waiting at the door. He apologises for the lift, which is out of order, and says that they will have to climb to the third floor. Zilola does not mind, but Mark, who is carrying a heavy bag, sighs loudly.

Inside, the flat is bright, and the living room faces south. Peter explains that the rent is six hundred and fifty pounds a month, and that the advertisement, which said five hundred and sixty, contained a mistake. Zilola is a little annoyed, because she had planned her budget around the lower number. Peter says the owner might accept six hundred if she signs for a full year, but he cannot promise anything. Zilola replies that she will think about it, although she says she is not hopeful.

The kitchen is small but modern, with a new oven and a washing machine. However, there is no dishwasher, and Peter says the owner will not install one. In the bedroom there is a large built-in wardrobe, which Zilola likes very much, but the window looks onto a busy road. She asks whether it is noisy at night. Peter says that it is quiet after eleven, though Mark points out that a lorry has just passed and the glass trembled. Peter smiles uncomfortably and says that double glazing will be fitted next spring.

The agent then goes through the conditions. The deposit is equal to one month's rent, and it is returned at the end of the contract if nothing is damaged. Pets are not allowed, except for fish, which Mark finds funny. Bills are not included, apart from water, so Zilola must also pay for electricity and the internet. The shortest contract is six months, and she can leave early only if she gives two months' notice.

On the way down, Zilola tells Mark that she has mixed feelings. She loves the light and the wardrobe, and the park is only five minutes away. But the price is more than she wanted, and she is worried about the noise. Mark advises her to visit again in the evening, which she thinks is a good idea. Before they leave, she asks Peter whether there is another flat available in the same building. He says there is one on the first floor, slightly smaller, for six hundred pounds, but it will not be free until next month. Zilola says she will call him on Thursday with her decision, and she asks him not to show the flat to anyone else before then, if possible.
