Zilola and her friend Mark arrive at a small block of flats near the park at four o'clock, and the agent, a young man called Peter, is already waiting at the door. He apologises for the lift, which is out of order, and says that they will have to climb to the third floor. Zilola does not mind, but Mark, who is carrying a heavy bag, sighs loudly.

Inside, the flat is bright, and the living room faces south. Peter explains that the rent is six hundred and fifty pounds a month, and that the advertisement, which said five hundred and sixty, contained a mistake. Zilola is a little annoyed, because she had planned her budget around the lower number. Peter says the owner might accept six hundred if she signs for a full year, but he cannot promise anything. Zilola replies that she will think about it, although she says she is not hopeful.

The kitchen is small but modern, with a new oven and a washing machine. However, there is no dishwasher, and Peter says the owner will not install one. In the bedroom there is a large built-in wardrobe, which Zilola likes very much, but the window looks onto a busy road. She asks whether it is noisy at night. Peter says that it is quiet after eleven, though Mark points out that a lorry has just passed and the glass trembled. Peter smiles uncomfortably and says that double glazing will be fitted next spring.

The agent then goes through the conditions. The deposit is equal to one month's rent, and it is returned at the end of the contract if nothing is damaged. Pets are not allowed, except for fish, which Mark finds funny. Bills are not included, apart from water, so Zilola must also pay for electricity and the internet. The shortest contract is six months, and she can leave early only if she gives two months' notice.

On the way down, Zilola tells Mark that she has mixed feelings. She loves the light and the wardrobe, and the park is only five minutes away. But the price is more than she wanted, and she is worried about the noise. Mark advises her to visit again in the evening, which she thinks is a good idea. Before they leave, she asks Peter whether there is another flat available in the same building. He says there is one on the first floor, slightly smaller, for six hundred pounds, but it will not be free until next month. Zilola says she will call him on Thursday with her decision, and she asks him not to show the flat to anyone else before then, if possible.

items.prompt: What is Timur's latest maths result?
items.audio:
On Thursday evening Gulnora Ergasheva goes to her son's school to meet his class teacher, Mr Patel. Her son Timur is fourteen, and she has been worried about him since the autumn. She sits down, thanks the teacher for his time, and says she hopes the news is not too bad.

Mr Patel smiles and says that, on the whole, it is better than she thinks. He begins with mathematics, where Timur has improved a great deal. At the start of the year he was getting forty percent in tests, but his last result was seventy-five. The teacher believes that the extra lessons on Tuesday afternoons have made the difference. Gulnora is delighted and says she was not sure whether Timur was even going to those lessons. Mr Patel confirms that he has missed only one.

However, there are problems in other subjects. In history Timur has handed in only three of the seven homework tasks, and the last essay was copied from the internet. The teacher says he is not accusing Timur of cheating on purpose, because he might not understand that copying is wrong, but he must learn quickly. Gulnora is embarrassed and promises to speak to him. She asks whether he should be punished at school. Mr Patel says no, not this time, but a second case would mean a meeting with the head teacher.

Then they talk about behaviour. Timur is generally polite, and the other pupils like him, but he talks too much in class, especially when he sits next to his friend Jasur. The teacher has decided to move them to different desks, and he hopes this will help without any further action. Gulnora says she is not surprised, because Timur talks all the time at home, too, unless he is looking at his phone.

Gulnora raises the subject of next year. Timur says he wants to study computer science, and she wonders whether he should drop art to concentrate on maths and physics. Mr Patel disagrees. He says art is the one subject in which Timur is truly relaxed and creative, and universities like to see a wide range of interests. He suggests keeping art but dropping geography, in which Timur has no interest and gets only average marks.

At the end, the teacher gives her a list of three websites for practising mathematics and asks her to limit his phone use to one hour on school nights. Gulnora promises to try. She says she will come again in March, not in June as she did last year, because she wants to be sure that the history problem has been solved.

items.prompt: Why is Sarah coming home in July?
items.audio:
Gulnora has not spoken to her friend Sarah for almost three years, so when Sarah calls on Sunday evening, they both start laughing before they can say hello. They were classmates at university in Samarkand, and then Sarah moved to Canada to work for an insurance company. They promised to stay in touch, but life, as always, got in the way.

Sarah says that she is calling because she is coming home in July for her cousin's wedding. At first she tells Gulnora that she will stay for two weeks, then she changes her mind and says that three weeks is more realistic, because her boss has agreed to let her work from home for the last one. Gulnora is thrilled and offers her spare room, but Sarah politely refuses. She says her parents would be offended if she stayed anywhere else, and anyway, she wants to save her friend from her snoring.

Gulnora asks about Canada. Sarah says that the winters are harder than she imagined, and for the first year she hated them. The pay is much better than at home, but rent is very high, and she spends almost half her salary on a tiny flat. She says that she sometimes thinks about coming back for good, but her partner, Daniel, has a good job and does not want to move. Gulnora asks whether they plan to marry. Sarah hesitates, then says that they are engaged but have not told anyone, so Gulnora must keep it secret. Gulnora promises, although she admits that she is terrible at secrets.

Then Sarah asks about Gulnora's life. Gulnora explains that she left the bank two years ago and now teaches economics at a private college. She earns less, but she likes the work, and she is also studying for a master's degree in the evenings. She says that it is exhausting, because she often goes to bed after midnight. Sarah is impressed and says that she herself gave up the idea of a master's degree, because the tuition would have cost her thirty thousand dollars.

They decide to meet in the capital on the second Saturday of July, but Gulnora remembers that she has exams that weekend, so they agree to meet on the Sunday instead. Before they hang up, Sarah says that she is bringing a present, and she refuses to say what it is. Gulnora guesses that it is chocolate, which Sarah neither confirms nor denies. They say goodbye after an hour and a half, and both feel that the call was far too short.

items.prompt: What does the speaker say about the audience at his talks?
items.answer: Some look worried and some bored
items.audio:
Thank you for coming, everyone. I have been giving this talk for eight years, and it is always the same. Half of you look worried, and the other half look bored. Let me say right now that the bored half should listen very carefully, because student loans are not as simple as they appear.

First, the basics. A student loan is money that you borrow to pay for tuition and living costs. Unlike a bank loan, you do not start paying it back until you earn above a certain amount. At present that amount is twenty-seven thousand pounds a year. If you earn less, you pay nothing, and if you earn more, you pay nine percent of the part above the threshold, not nine percent of your whole salary. Many students misunderstand this. So a graduate earning thirty thousand pounds pays nine percent of three thousand pounds, which is two hundred and seventy pounds a year, or about twenty-two pounds a month.

Second, interest. The loan grows while you are studying, and this is the part that frightens people. A student who borrows forty thousand pounds may owe fifty thousand by graduation. But, and this is important, whether you ever repay all of it depends mainly on your salary, not on the size of the debt. After thirty years, any balance remaining is cancelled. For a lot of average earners that means that they will never pay it all back, so in practice the loan behaves more like a tax than a debt.

Third, a warning. This system applies to home students only. If you are an international student, you cannot get this kind of loan, and you will need a private lender, whose conditions are very different. Private loans have to be repaid in full, with no cancellation, and the rate may change. I would be careful there. Several students who sat where you are sitting now borrowed privately and regretted it.

Some of you will ask whether it is better to work during your degree instead of borrowing. My honest answer is that a few hours a week is useful, but more than fifteen hours often damages your marks. I have seen students lose a whole grade because they worked every evening. And whatever you do, do not take extra credit for things you do not need, such as the latest phone.

Now, questions. I see a hand at the back. Yes, about the thirty years. Does it start from graduation or from the first payment? It starts in the April after you finish your course, even if you were unemployed at the time. I will finish by saying that borrowing for education is rarely a mistake, but borrowing without understanding is.
options: Some look worried and some bored

items.prompt: How many guests did Nigora say the list had reached?
items.audio:
Bobur and his fiancée Nigora sit down with a wedding planner called Mrs Ahmedova on a rainy Tuesday morning. They have been engaged for six months, and their families have strong opinions about everything. Mrs Ahmedova opens her notebook and asks them to begin with the number of guests.

Bobur says that they have written a list of one hundred and fifty people, but Nigora immediately disagrees. She says that, after talking with her mother, the list has grown to one hundred and eighty, because of distant relatives who would be offended if they were not invited. Bobur is surprised and says that he never agreed to this, and that they cannot afford it. Mrs Ahmedova suggests a compromise. A hundred and twenty guests for the main dinner, and a larger group invited only to the evening party. The couple look at each other and, after a pause, agree.

Next is the venue. Nigora would like a garden by the river, but Mrs Ahmedova warns that the weather in September is unpredictable, and a tent would cost an extra two thousand pounds. Bobur prefers a restaurant in the city centre, which has a hall for a hundred and thirty people. The hall costs five thousand pounds, including food, which is a lot cheaper than the garden. Nigora is not completely convinced, but she accepts it because she cares more about the photographs than about the building. Mrs Ahmedova promises to ask the photographer whether he can take pictures in the park next to the restaurant.

The discussion turns to the budget. Their parents are contributing ten thousand pounds, and the couple have saved four thousand themselves. Mrs Ahmedova points out that this is enough for the dinner, music and flowers, but not for the honeymoon, which Bobur had also hoped to include. After some thought, Bobur says that they will postpone the honeymoon until the spring and go away for just a weekend now. Nigora is happy with the idea, although she says she would have chosen the beach.

Then they come to the date. Originally, they wanted the fourteenth of September, but Mrs Ahmedova checks her diary and says that the restaurant is already booked on that day. The twenty-first is free. Bobur's brother cannot come on the twenty-first because he has an exam, but Bobur says that this cannot be helped. Finally, the planner asks whether there will be any speeches. Nigora says only one, by her grandfather, and she asks everyone to keep it short. They all laugh, and the meeting finishes with a list of tasks for next week.

Bobur says that they have written a list of one hundred and fifty people, but Nigora immediately disagrees. She says that, after talking with her mother, the list has grown to one hundred and eighty, because of distant relatives who would be offended if they were not invited. Bobur is surprised and says that he never agreed to this, and that they cannot afford it. Mrs Ahmedova suggests a compromise. A hundred and twenty guests for the main dinner, and a larger group invited only to the evening party. The couple look at each other and, after a pause, agree.

Next is the venue. Nigora would like a garden by the river, but Mrs Ahmedova warns that the weather in September is unpredictable, and a tent would cost an extra two thousand pounds. Bobur prefers a restaurant in the city centre, which has a hall for a hundred and thirty people. The hall costs five thousand pounds, including food, which is a lot cheaper than the garden. Nigora is not completely convinced, but she accepts it because she cares more about the photographs than about the building. Mrs Ahmedova promises to ask the photographer whether he can take pictures in the park next to the restaurant.

The discussion turns to the budget. Their parents are contributing ten thousand pounds, and the couple have saved four thousand themselves. Mrs Ahmedova points out that this is enough for the dinner, music and flowers, but not for the honeymoon, which Bobur had also hoped to include. After some thought, Bobur says that they will postpone the honeymoon until the spring and go away for just a weekend now. Nigora is happy with the idea, although she says she would have chosen the beach.

Then they come to the date. Originally, they wanted the fourteenth of September, but Mrs Ahmedova checks her diary and says that the restaurant is already booked on that day. The twenty-first is free. Bobur's brother cannot come on the twenty-first because he has an exam, but Bobur says that this cannot be helped. Finally, the planner asks whether there will be any speeches. Nigora says only one, by her grandfather, and she asks everyone to keep it short. They all laugh, and the meeting finishes with a list of tasks for next week.
items.explain: The hall costs five thousand including food, while the garden needs an extra tent.

items.prompt: What is Karim's problem at the start?
items.answer: He cannot explain where his salary went
items.audio:
Every Friday afternoon, Karim meets his mentor, a retired finance manager called Mrs Lawson, in a quiet cafe near his office. Karim is twenty-four and has just started his first proper job at a software company. This Friday he arrives looking worried, and before he has even ordered his tea, he tells her that he received his first salary and cannot understand where it all went.

Mrs Lawson laughs kindly and says that this is the most normal problem in the world. She asks him to take out his phone and look at his bank statement. Together they discover that Karim paid six hundred pounds for rent, two hundred and forty for food, and a surprising ninety for taxis, although his office is only fifteen minutes from his flat on foot. Karim admits that he took taxis because he was always late. Mrs Lawson does not criticise him. She simply says that getting up thirty minutes earlier is the cheapest investment he will ever make.

Then she gives him three pieces of advice. The first is to pay himself first. On the day his salary arrives, he should move ten percent into a savings account before he spends anything. Karim says that ten percent seems a lot, and she answers that he can begin with five and increase it gradually, but he must begin. The second is to say yes to a pension scheme, which his company offers, and which will add money on top of his own. Karim says he thought pensions were for old people. She tells him that this is the biggest mistake of young workers, because time is what makes the money grow.

The third piece of advice is not about money at all. She tells him to ask for a performance review after six months and to prepare a list of everything he has achieved. Karim worries that asking for a raise might look greedy. Mrs Lawson says that it is not greedy, it is professional, though she warns him not to ask in the same week that he makes a mistake, which, she says, she learned the hard way.

Towards the end, Karim mentions that his friend has offered him a share in a restaurant business, promising high profits. Mrs Lawson becomes serious. She says that she would not invest in anything that she did not understand or that a friend was pressing her to decide quickly. She suggests that he asks to see the accounts and talks to a lawyer first. Karim nods, writes it down, and promises to tell her what happens next Friday.

items.prompt: How much was the monthly allowance?
items.audio:
Hello, everyone. My name is Anvar, and I am going to talk for about ten minutes about the year I spent studying in Germany, which I did last year as part of an exchange programme. items.prompt: How much of the deposit does Mr Brown first plan to return?
items.audio:
Sevara rented a small flat for one year, and when the contract ended last week, she moved out and cleaned the place thoroughly. Now she is on the phone with her landlord, Mr Brown, because he has told her that he will keep a part of her deposit. The deposit was seven hundred pounds, and he says that he plans to return only four hundred and fifty.

Mr Brown begins by listing the reasons. First, there is a mark on the living room carpet, which he says was not there when she moved in. Second, one of the kitchen cupboard doors is loose. Third, the oven was not clean enough. Sevara listens quietly and then answers each point. She says that the carpet mark was already there in the first week, and that she remembers sending him a photograph by email in September. She is sure the email is still in her inbox. As for the cupboard, she says that the hinge was already weak and that she had told him about it in the spring, though he never sent anyone to repair it.

Mr Brown pauses and admits that he does not remember the email, but he insists that the oven was dirty. Sevara disagrees strongly. She says she spent two hours cleaning it, and she took photographs of everything on the day she left. She offers to send them. Mr Brown says that this might change things, and he would like to see them. However, he warns her that he does not accept photographs taken on a phone as proof. Sevara points out that he told her to take pictures in the first place, in the contract itself, and Mr Brown goes quiet.

He finally suggests a compromise. He will keep fifty pounds for the oven and return six hundred and fifty. Sevara considers this carefully. She says that she does not want to start an argument, but she also does not want to lose money for something she did not do. Instead of accepting at once, she proposes that they ask an independent organisation which looks after deposits to decide. Mr Brown does not like the idea, because it could take up to six weeks, but he admits that it is fair.

In the end, they agree to wait until Sevara sends the photographs and the old email, and Mr Brown promises to give his answer by Friday. Sevara thanks him, but she says politely that if she does not hear from him by then, she will contact the organisation herself. After the call she feels tired, but also proud that she stayed calm, which was not easy.

items.prompt: How old is the couple's daughter?
items.audio:
Ilhom and his wife Dilfuza visit a financial adviser called Mr Clarke because they cannot decide whether to buy a flat or keep renting. They are both thirty-one, and they have a daughter who is almost three. Their savings amount to twenty-two thousand pounds, and their combined income is five thousand pounds a month before tax.

Mr Clarke begins by saying that the question is not as simple as most people believe. He knows that many families think that renting is throwing money away, but he does not agree. When you rent, he explains, you are paying for flexibility and freedom from repair costs, and there are times in life when that is worth the price. When you buy, you build up something that belongs to you, but you also take on risks, such as rising interest rates, repairs and the possibility that the price of the property falls.

Dilfuza asks how big a loan they could get. Mr Clarke says that most banks will lend about four times a yearly income, which in their case could be one hundred and forty thousand pounds if the bank considers their jobs secure. However, he adds that borrowing the maximum is rarely wise. He recommends keeping the monthly payment below thirty percent of their income, and that would mean about fifteen hundred pounds. Ilhom looks at his wife with concern, because that is nearly double their present rent.

Then Mr Clarke talks about the deposit. Banks usually want ten percent of the price, but a larger deposit means lower interest. With twenty-two thousand pounds they could afford a flat costing two hundred thousand, but he warns that they should not use all their savings, because they also need money for legal fees, furniture and an emergency fund. Ilhom says that they had not thought about legal fees. Mr Clarke smiles and says that almost nobody does.

He then offers a different option. He suggests that they continue renting for two more years while they save an extra ten thousand pounds, and meanwhile watch the market. Ilhom thinks this is sensible, but Dilfuza is not sure. She is worried that prices might rise in the meantime, which would make the dream flat even more expensive. Mr Clarke admits that nobody can predict the market, and he would not tell them to wait if they could comfortably afford to buy now. But in their situation, he thinks, patience is cheaper than regret.

At the end, the couple say they will talk it over at home. Mr Clarke gives them a list of questions to discuss and a calculator on his website. He reminds them that his advice is free for the first meeting only. Dilfuza thanks him and says they will come back in a month, probably with more doubts than answers.

items.prompt: How much does Sherzod want to borrow?
items.audio:
Late on Saturday evening, Feruza sits at the kitchen table with her husband Oleg, and the conversation is not an easy one. Her younger brother Sherzod has asked to borrow three thousand pounds to open a small shop that sells mobile phone accessories. He was supposed to come for dinner tonight, but he cancelled at the last minute, and Feruza suspects that he is embarrassed.

Oleg says that he likes Sherzod, but he does not think they should lend the money. He reminds his wife that, two years ago, they lent him five hundred pounds for a motorbike, and he returned only half of it. Feruza answers that Sherzod was only twenty then, and he has changed. He now has a steady job at a car repair garage and has saved a thousand pounds himself. Oleg is not convinced and points out that the most likely reason for a new business to fail is not laziness but lack of experience, and Sherzod has never run a shop.

Feruza looks tired and says that she does not want to ruin her relationship with her brother over money. Oleg replies that this is exactly the point, since lending to family can damage relationships much more than refusing. He tells her about his cousin, who lent money to a friend and has not spoken to him for six years. Feruza thinks this is an exaggeration, but she lowers her voice and agrees that the story is sad.

After some silence, Oleg suggests a different approach. Instead of giving all three thousand pounds, they could lend one thousand five hundred and sign a simple written agreement, with monthly repayments of one hundred pounds beginning after six months. Feruza likes the idea, although she says it feels cold to ask a brother to sign a paper. Oleg says that it protects both sides, because nobody can later say that they misunderstood what was agreed.

Then Feruza raises a practical point. Their own savings are meant for the new roof, and a loan of fifteen hundred would leave very little. Oleg says that he is willing to delay the roof until next autumn, as the old one has survived many winters. They also agree to ask Sherzod to show them a business plan, with expected costs and the rent of the shop.

Finally, Feruza calls her brother, and he answers on the second ring. She tells him the plan and, to her relief, Sherzod is not offended. He says that he would have asked for a written agreement himself, and he will come over on Sunday to talk, and this time, he promises, he will not cancel.

items.prompt: How did Laylo get the job?
items.answer: She offered help when the owner complained
items.audio:
Last summer, Laylo, who was sixteen, got her first paid job in a bakery near her home, and she is now telling her cousin Ben about the experience over a video call. Ben is considering a similar job and has many questions, so he asks her to start at the beginning.

Laylo says that she found the job almost by accident. She walked into the bakery to buy bread, and the owner, Mrs Rossi, was complaining to a customer that her assistant had left without warning. Laylo, who was embarrassed but brave, asked whether she needed help. Mrs Rossi looked at her for a moment and said that she could start on Monday at six o'clock in the morning. Laylo, who had never woken up before eight in her life, said yes before she thought about it.

The first week was difficult. She had to carry heavy bags of flour, serve customers who were often rude because they had not yet drunk their coffee, and learn the names of thirty different kinds of bread. By Thursday, she was so exhausted that she fell asleep on the bus and missed her stop. However, she says that by the second week she felt stronger and more confident, and the early mornings became surprisingly pleasant. She loved watching the town wake up, and she often ate a warm roll while the street was still silent.

Ben asks about the pay. Laylo explains that she was paid six pounds an hour, which is the legal minimum for her age, and she worked twenty hours a week. After tax, she saved about three hundred pounds a month.
